1071. Definition of a Foreign Corporation 

When a private corporation is created, it enjoys certain rights and privileges not enjoyed by natural persons. Because of this fact, the private corporation has become an important factor in the business world. All authorities agree that the right to be a corporation is not a natural right of a person or a group of persons. It is a right existing only by authority of the sovereign. 

Such authority may be expressed or implied.¹

No state of the United States has governmental power or control over the other states. Inasmuch as each state's sovereignty is limited to its own territory, the question arises as to whether a private corporation which comes into existence and survives only by and with the consent of a state can function as a corporation outside the boundaries of the state of its creation. In an early United States Supreme Court case it was held that a corporation can have no legal existence outside the boundaries of the sovereignty by which it is created. It exists only in contemplation of law, and by force of the law; and where that law ceases to operate, and is no longer obligatory, the corporation can have no existence. "It must dwell in the place of its creation, and cannot migrate to another sovereignty." Even when that

classical statement was written by the Supreme Court of the United States it was more in the nature of the statement of a fiction or a metaphor, rather than of a real fact. As we will see throughout this chapter it is no longer true that the business of a corporation is confined to the state in which it was incorporated. 

Our purpose in this chapter is to deal with the rights, privileges, and immunities of foreign corporations. At the outset, we must first determine just what is meant by the term "foreign corporation." A foreign corporation may be defined as one that derives its existence from the authority of another state, government, or country. Therefore, so far as Texas is concerned all corporations organized or created under the laws of any other state or nation, or of any territory of the United States, are foreign corporations. And when they come to Texas and "transact business," they are treated as "foreign corporations." 3 

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1529 defines a foreign corporation as one "organized or created under the law of any other state, or any territory of the United States, or of any municipality of such State or Territory, or of any foreign government, sovereignty or municipality." Corporations created by Congress with powers co-extensive with the boundaries of the United States are not foreign corporations within any state of the Union. The 

Home Owners' Loan Corporation was organized under an Act of Congress. It is not a foreign corporation while doing business in Texas. Therefore, it need not take out a permit before transacting business in Texas.5

Ch. § 1072 

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1072. Is a Foreign Statutory Association or Joint-Stock Com pany a Foreign Corporation?

In some states statutes have been passed authorizing the creation of associations that possess most, if not all, the advantages of the corporation, but these associations are not denominated corporations by the statute under which they are organized. In 

Pennsylvania by the Act of June 2, 1874, 59 P.S. § 341 et seq., "partnership associations limited" may be organized with limited liability of its members and all other advantages of the corporation except that a transferee of a share of the stock of the association is not entitled to any participation in the subsequent business of the association unless he is elected to membership by a vote of a majority of the members."

In the case cited in the last note Judge Lurton for the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals held that such associations are corporations. The question involved in that case was whether such associations could sue in the federal courts on the ground of diversity of citizenship. Judge Lurton held that they are corporations and could sue in the federal court in a state other than Pennsylvania. He argued that under the Pennsylvania statute the shareholders are formed into a separate legal personality. 

In the case of Great Southern Fire Proof Hotel Co. v. Jones 10 

the Supreme Court of the United States refused "to concur" with Judge Lurton, but the latter Court gave no reason for its position except that "We are unwilling to extend it (rule of suing a federal court on the ground of diversity of citizenship) so as to embrace partnership associations." merce, being in the federal government, is not to be restricted by state authority.' Appellant relies upon the language in the above quotation, 'where the corporation is in the employ of the federal government,' as being authority for its exemption from our statutes above cited. But we think appellant was not 'in the employ of the federal government' in the sense there used. It was under contract with the government to do a specific job in a certain way, using its own equipment and hiring its own employees, a typical case of independent contractor, and the ordinary relation of employer and employee, master and servant, principal and agent did not exist between it and the government. 

That it is an independent contractor and is not a government instrumentality there can be no doubt."

Coke Co., C.C.A.Ohio, 86 F. 585, 58 U.S.Appeals 444. 10.

The opinion of Judge Lurton is better reasoned than that of Judge Harlan, and will be followed by the Texas Supreme Court in determining whether such associations, and similar associations organized under the laws of a foreign state or nation, are foreign corporations within the meaning of the Texas statutes when they come to Texas and transact intrastate business. This question has not been decided by any of the Texas courts.11 In deciding that question, the court will compare the statute of the foreign state or nation under which the "association" or "statutory joint-stock company" was organized with the Texas general incorporation statute, and if the foreign company has most, or all, of the advantages of the Texas corporation, the courts of Texas will hold that it is a foreign corporation, and, therefore, the association should take out a permit if it wishes to transact intrastate business in Texas.12 

§ 1073. Rights of Foreign Corporations That Obtain Permits 

The Texas statute provides that when a foreign corporation complies with the Texas law and obtains a permit it "shall have and enjoy all the rights and privileges conferred by the laws of this state on corporations organized under the laws of this state.' FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

A foreign corporation that has authority under its charter to go surety on a guardian's bond may exercise that authority in Texas.15 Where the contract of insurance by a foreign corporation makes the charter and the laws of the state where the company was incorporated parts of the policy, the Texas Courts will follow the construction of such laws by the Supreme Court of the State where the company was organized.¹ 16 As long as the local law is not violated, a foreign corporation in transacting business in Texas may make its charter, by-laws, rules, and regulations part of a contract entered into in Texas. 

Where that is provided for in the contract the other party is charged with notice of the provisions of these instruments.17 If a foreign corporation is organized under the general incorporation statutes of another state those laws and its charter determine its powers, but it does not bring to Texas all of the statutory laws of the state where the company was incorporated.18 

Since by the express provisions of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 

1532, a foreign corporation has all the rights of a domestic corporation where it has obtained a permit to do business in Texas, it can sue another foreign corporation that is transacting business in Texas on a transitory cause of action that arose outside the borders of Texas, but such a corporation does not become "a citizen" of Texas.19 § 1074. Ch. § 1075 

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

the Supreme Court of the United States has held that an unincorporated labor union is an artificial person capable of suing and being sued 24 yet the lower federal courts still hold that an unincorporated association cannot sue in the federal courts on the ground of diversity of citizenship. This question was not involved in the United Mine Worker's case as that was a suit under the Federal Anti-Trust Statute, and the jurisdiction of the federal courts was based on a specific provision of the statute and not on the ground of diversity of citizenship.25 The opinion holding that a large labor union could be sued as an entity is based largely on the fact that Congress by reason of several statutes had recognized the separate existence of labor unions. For this reason that case cannot be cited to show that an unincorporated association at common law can sue and be sued. 

§ 1075. Power of Foreign Corporations to Act in Another Juris diction-Comity

It is conceded everywhere that the states have the power to prohibit the entrance of foreign corporations into their separate jurisdictions with certain exceptions. However, the prevailing view is that such foreign corporations whose business is not contrary to the statutes, constitutions or the public policy of a particular state will be admitted.26 This is in keeping with the doctrine of comity. If a state has no legislation on entrance requirements, it is generally held that a corporation of another state can function in the same capacity and as freely as domes-

Ch. § 1076 

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1076. The Right to Exclude or Impose Conditions 

Prior to July 3, 1889, foreign corporations enjoyed unrestricted rights to enter into any business in this state for which a corporation could be created in Texas.30 The statute of 1887, relating to foreign corporations, was declared unconstitutional.31 As a result from 1887 until 1889 there was no effective statute concerning foreign corporations, and they were on an equal footing with domestic corporations during such period.32 But since 1889, foreign corporations have been forced to meet certain statutory regulations before being permitted to transact business in Texas.33 

In Texas, any corporation for pecuniary profit, organized or created under the laws of any other state, or of any territory of the United States, or of any municipality of such state or territory, or of any foreign government, sovereignty or municipality, (1) desiring to transact, or (2) solicit business in Texas, or (3) to establish a general or special office in this State, shall file with the Secretary of State a duly certified copy of its articles of incorporation; and thereupon such official shall issue to such corporation a permit to transact business in this State for a period of ten years from the date of so filing such articles of incorporation. 

If such corporation is created for more than one purpose, the permit may be limited to one or more purposes.34 "Before such permit is issued such corporation shall show to the satisfaction of the Secretary of State that at least one hundred thousand dollars in cash of their authorized capital stock has been paid in, or that fifty per cent of their authorized capital stock has been subscribed, and at least ten per cent thereof paid in." 35

Before a permit is issued to such corporation, its president, vice president, secretary or treasurer, or two of the directors, must file an affidavit stating that such corporation is not a trust, or organization in restraint of trade in violation of the laws of Texas; also that said corporation has not within twelve months next preceding the making of such affidavit, become or been a party to any trust agreement of any kind which would constitute a violation of any anti-trust law of Texas existing at the date of such affidavit, and has not within that time, entered into or been in any wise a party to, any combination in restraint of trade within the United States, and that no officer of such corporation has, within the knowledge of the affiant, within such time and on behalf of such corporation or for its benefit, made any such contract, or entered into or become a party to any such combination in restraint of trade.36 "Such corporations, on obtaining such permit, shall have and enjoy all the rights and privileges conferred by the laws of this state on corporations organized under the laws of this State." 37 "Each foreign corporation, after a permit has been granted it to do business in this State, shall immediately file with the Secretary of State a certified copy of any amendment or supplement to its original articles of incorporation when any such amendment or supplement to its original articles of incorporation is filed in the state territory or foreign country under whose laws such corporation is incorporated." 38 

The statutes on foreign corporations do not apply to corporations created for the purpose of constructing, building, operating or maintaining any railway, or to such corporations as are required by law to procure certificates of authority to do business from the Commissioner of Insurance or from the Banking Commissioner.39 But when the foreign corporation is suing a railroad company in a Texas Court and the plaintiff is not a railroad the statute with reference to obtaining a permit applies.40

According to S. R. Smythe Co. v. Ft. Worth Glass & Sand Co.,41 the purpose of these statutes was twofold: 1. To protect the people of this state from irresponsible foreign corporations, by affording them the means of ascertaining such information as is contained in their charters. 2. The other purpose was to put foreign corporations on the same footing as similar domestic corporations by requiring them to pay a fee for a permit to do business in Texas as domestic corporations are required to do to obtain a charter. 

According to Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1529, only foreign "corporations for pecuniary profit" that "transact or solicit business in Texas" are required to take out a permit. A foreign corporation for benevolent, religious or philanthropic purposes where the charter provides that all of its revenues except reasonable expenses will be devoted to one or more of such purposes is not organized "for pecuniary profit." Such a corporation does not come within the provision of the Texas statutes, and, therefore, could recover on a claim due it without proving that it obtained a permit. A corporation organized for the above purpose has authority to buy land reasonably necessary to further its chartered powers.42

The Texas Legislature can provide that foreign corporations be forced to deposit securities with the Texas Commissioner of 

Banking and that these assets cannot be removed from Texas until the Texas creditors are paid.43 But when it ceases to do business in Texas and has paid all of its obligations to local creditors, it has a right to withdraw all securities deposited with any state official. The courts will not force the corporation to leave the sureties in Texas for the Texas shareholders.44

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1077. Constitutional Limitations 

There are, of course, certain constitutional limitations which the State of Texas must observe in the formation of statutes relative to foreign corporations. It has been held that a state can arbitrarily exclude a foreign corporation unless it is engaged in interstate commerce or performing some government function,45 and hence, subject to these limitations, a state, as a general rule, can impose any requirements for admission that it chooses, provided that they are not contra to either the state or federal constitutions.46 The right of the state to impose restrictions on foreign corporations, however, is being continually restricted by judicial decision. The prohibition against denying to the citizens of any state the privileges and immunities of citizens in the several states of our Federal constitution does not prevent a state from excluding a corporation, created in another state. This article applies to the privileges and immunities enjoyed by the citizens in common in their separate states, and not to special privileges granted them.47 A foreign corporation is a person within the constitutional provision that no state shall deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.4

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1078. Foreign Corporations in Fraud of the Laws of a State, or 

Contrary to Its Policy The courts of a state will not recognize as valid a corporation organized in fraud of its laws in another state, or a corporation of another state which is contrary to the policy of its laws.64 In some states the laws for the formation of corporations are more favorable than in others, and for this reason, residents of a state sometimes go into another state and form a corporation under its laws for the purpose of doing business in the state of their residence. Whether such corporations will be recognized as valid in the state of the corporators' residence depends upon whether the incorporation is to be regarded as an evasion of and fraud upon its laws.65 Some courts seem to hold that the mere fact that residents of a state go into another state and form a corporation for the purpose of doing business in the state of their residence is an evasion of the laws of the state in which they are incorporated, and a fraud upon such laws.66 But, by the better opinion, there must be something more than this to make out a case of fraud upon the laws of either state. There must be some express prohibition against such an incorporation, or else the general policy of the laws must be against it. The practice of forming a corporation under the laws of some state other than Texas by citizens of this state is common in Texas and is not condemned by our courts." Nor has our Texas Legislature

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1079. Powers of Foreign Corporation-Limitation of Charter 

The rule of comity by which a corporation created in one state is permitted to do business in another state does not change its nature as a foreign corporation, or give it any powers which are not included in its charter.79 Nor does it exempt persons who deal with it from the effect of legislation by the state where the company was created under power reserved by that law. "Though permitted to come into the local jurisdiction and there exercise its powers, for the accomplishment of the purposes of its creation, it remains essentially a foreign corporation. It derives its vitality, its corporate capacity, its very life, from the law of its origin. Comity adds to it no new function, or greater powers than are bestowed upon it by its charter. That, being the instrument of the company's creation and prescribing the limits of its legal existence, must exert the most obvious influence upon all its transactions; and, whether abroad or at home, it can do nothing which does not fairly fall within the scope and purpose of that instrument.” 80 And persons dealing with a foreign corporation must take notice of the limitations in its charter, and also of the power over it reserved to the state or country to which it owes its being, and they are bound accordingly.81 If the charter of a corporation or the general laws of the state of its creation prohibit certain contracts, as contracts between it and its officers or employees, the prohibition applies to contracts

The charter alone of the foreign corporation is recognized under the rule of comity, and not the general legislation of the state in which the corporation is formed.84 Such legislation has no extra-territorial force. Thus the New York statute law prohibiting preferential treatment of certain creditors in contemplation of insolvency has no force or application in Illinois.85 

If a foreign corporation whose existence and legal organization are not disputed has made a contract in a state through agents employed by it, and a suit is brought against it thereon in such state, in such a manner that it is made amenable to the jurisdiction of the court, it is not necessary for the plaintiff, at the outset, to prove that it had power under its charter to make the contract.86

In Texas the rule, that one who contracts with a corporation cannot plead ultra vires to defeat an action on the contract, and that the corporation is estopped to set up such a defense in an action brought against it, where the contract has been executed on the side of the party suing, applies to foreign corporations.87

§ 1080. Limitations of the Local Laws 

It does not follow, even when a corporation is recognized in another state, that it can exercise all the powers that are conferred upon it by its charter. Its powers also depend upon the law of the state in which they are exercised. In other words, its powers are limited, not only by its charter and the laws of the state of its creation, but also by the laws of the state in which it exercises them.91 Thus, a usurious contract was held invalid, although by its terms performance was to be in the parent state which had no usury laws. The court held the provision for performance outside the state was a mere devise to evade our usury laws,92 and that the contract was governed by our laws. A for-

§ 1082. Corporations de Facto 

A foreign corporation will be accorded the status of a corporation de facto, if it is a corporation de facto in the state by which it was created, and if it has complied with the law relating to foreign corporations. In such a case, persons who deal with it cannot attack its corporate existence on the ground of irregularity in organization.¹ Any question affecting its right to transact business because of such irregularity is a matter of inquiry only for the state of its creation.2

Ch. § 1086 

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1083. Rights and Immunities of Members 

The rights and immunities of members of foreign corporations are within the rule of comity, and must be respected. They cannot be held individually liable, for instance, for the debts or torts of the corporation, unless they are made so by its charter, or by some statute of the state where the corporation was organized.3 

§ 1084. Suits by the Attorney General 

Where a foreign corporation is transacting business in this state without a permit, the Attorney General is authorized to bring suit for penalties and to enjoin such action. The Attorney 

General is authorized to sue to cancel its permit where the corporation is insolvent 5 or has violated our anti-trust statutes. 

§ 1085. Mandamus to Secretary of State 

Where a foreign corporation offers to comply with our laws, mandamus will lie to compel the Secretary of State to issue it a permit."

State. To determine whether a foreign corporation is transacting business in this state is often difficult. 

The statutes of most jurisdictions prohibit foreign corporations from "doing," "carrying on" or "engaging" in business in the state without compliance with the conditions of the statutes. 

To come within the inhibition of the statute a foreign corporation must carry on some substantial part of its ordinary business: within this state."

On the other hand, the Texas statute precludes suit by an unlicensed foreign corporation on only intrastate transactions, and it has been intimated that a single or isolated transaction constituted transacting business in the state, even where the action of the corporation did not indicate a purpose of continuity of conduct in that respect.10 In S. R. Smythe Co. v. Ft. Worth Glass & 

Sand Co.,11 the court said: "We do not desire to put too great stress upon the peculiar language of our statute, yet there seems to be a distinction in those statutes which require the permit of foreign corporations to be secured where they desire 'to do business,' and where they desire to 'transact business' in the state. 

The two terms are not necessarily synonymous. To do business in this state imports a carrying on of business of the corporation for the purposes of its organization, while the transaction of business in this state rather imports the idea of isolated transactions in the line, of course, of the purposes of its creation." 

However, in Miller v. Goodman 12 the Supreme Court said: "It is a case of sale, by a corporation, created by another state, of goods manufactured in that state and shipped into the State of

Applying this principle it has been held that the sale of a single piano stored in Texas was not transacting business in the state.13 In Phelps v. Jesse French & Sons Piano

In view of the above authorities, it appears that it cannot be confidently said that a single isolated transaction by a foreign corporation showing no intent to continue such conduct, constitutes "doing business" in Texas.

The above mentioned cases seem to hold that if the foreign corporation sends a traveling representative to solicit orders, which are to be filled out of the state and shipped to the purchaser, the State of Texas has no power to interfere with such contracts as they are interstate transactions.42 In some of the cases the foreign corporation agreed as part of the sale contract to send a special representative to train salesmen to sell the particular goods, or a special representative to solicit orders. In these last mentioned cases the courts seem to think that in some cases it is absolutely necessary to agree to send a technician or a special representative to do the things agreed to be done, in order to sell the goods, and that such agreement was merely incidental to the sale, and that since the sale was interstate commerce, the state had absolutely no power to interfere in such transactions.

In Browning v. City of Waycross the court said: "We are of the opinion that the court below was right in holding that the business of erecting lightning rods, under the circumstances disclosed, was within the regulating power of the State and not the subject of interstate commerce for the following reasons: (a) Because the affixing of lightning rods to houses was the carrying on of a business of a strictly local character. (b) Such business involved no question of the delivery of property shipped in interstate commerce or necessary to complete an interstate commerce transaction, but was solely a local act performed after interstate commerce had completely terminated."

A later case, York Manufacturing Co. v. Colley,51 held that a contract for the sale and installation of machinery for an ice plant, and the agreement on the part of the foreign corporation that it would send an engineer to supervise the installation, to be paid by the domestic corporation, involved intrastate business and could be regulated by the State of Texas. All machinery and materials furnished under this contract were shipped from outside the State of Texas. The foreign corporation sent an engineer pursuant to the contract, who remained during the work which lasted from July 13, 1912, until August 9, 1912, and charged $144 for his services. This engineer supervised the work incident to the erection and installation of the machinery. This court stated, following the Smythe case,52 that the foreign corporation contracted to engage in and did engage in the strictly local business of installing an ice manufacturing plant; but it was conceded that it contracted to engage in and did engage in the business of supervising and superintending the erection of an ice plant, and the court held that such business was local business. In either event, the court held that the contract called for the transaction of business in this state without having obtained a permit. of Civil Appeals.67 A very logical conclusion would be that Texas will in the future follow the test as laid down by the Supreme Court in the York case. However, this test is rather broad and leaves room for argument. The cost of the machinery, the cost of the installation, the length of time taken, and the amount of material purchased in this state, should be considered in applying the test.68 It would seem that if the machinery is of such a nature as to require expert supervision in its installation in order to produce the required results which the foreign corporation was bound to guarantee in order to accomplish the sale, the installation could be said to be incidental to the sale, and thus would constitute interstate commerce. Competition is keen, and in order to sell machinery the purchaser must be assured that it will give satisfaction. 

At the present time the market is crowded with machinery which can be said to be very sensitive, and which will require installation by technicians who possess knowledge and information which can be obtained only by diligent study of such machinery. If a local engineer is secured, although he is an expert, it is probable that he might not be able to make the particular machine function as required, and litigation would probably follow. Under such circumstances it seems logical to say that the installation is incidental to the sale.

In holding that the transaction was an interstate transaction, thereby permitting the corporation to sue in a Texas court without a permit, the Commission of Appeals said: "Our federal Constitution confers upon Congress the exclusive power to regulate interstate commerce, and the state is without authority to enact a law which would interfere with this power. 

The purchase of the gas plant to be transported from Indiana to this state was an interstate transaction, and one which the state by statutory enactment had no power to regulate or control by requiring a permit or denying the seller the right to institute suit in the courts of this state to enforce payment of the purchase price. "The right to make an interstate commerce contract', such as the one here involved, 'includes in its very terms the right to incorporate into such contract provisions which are relevant and appropriate to the contract made.' The agreement to supply materials and labor, whether from points within or without this state, for the purpose of installing the plant and thereby performing the obligation imposed under the terms of the contract, was relevant and appropriate to a transaction inherently interstate in character. The materials and labor supplied were essentially connected with the subject-matter of the sale. This case, in its facts, presents the question of law decided by the United 

States Supreme Court in the case of York Mfg. Co. v. Colley." "70 The authorities are carefully considered in the recent case of

On the other hand if the transaction is one in which the sale of a foreignmade product may be regarded rather as an incident of a contract for labor within the state, than as the chief incident of the transaction, the transaction falls within state control and is not protected by the commerce clause of the Federal Constitution." 74

It is very doubtful that the interpretation as to what is an isolated transaction is correct. If certain work is in fact incidental to interstate commerce, it makes no difference how great in number the work (transactions) may be; in each case the character remains the same. If installation work is merely incidental to such commerce, the accumulation in number cannot change the interstate commerce to intrastate." 79 installation is incidental and involves a small expense as compared to the purchase price of the article; and we are of the opinion that such agreements concerning transactions which otherwise would constitute interstate commerce do not remove them from that category and render them intrastate commerce. Upon that point, this case may not be fully developed, and therefore that issue will be left open in order that additional testimony, if desired, may be offered upon it."

Since the above decision in the Southern Discount Co. v. Rose case 80 was rendered, several important cases have been decided by our Courts of Civil Appeals and the Commission of Appeals. 

In Phelps v. Jesse French & Sons Piano Co.,81 the Dallas Court of 

Civil Appeals permitted recovery by the foreign corporation for the purchase price of four pianos that had been repossessed by the corporation from Texas purchasers and resold while they were still stored in Texas. In American Soda Fountain Co. V. 

Hairston,82 in its original opinion the Court of Civil Appeals at El Paso denied recovery by the foreign corporation upon notes given for a soda fountain and its equipment, but on motion for rehearing the original opinion was changed and the corporation was permitted to recover, the court citing the Phelps-Jesse French Co. case with approval. The subject matter of the sale was a soda fountain which was to be shipped from outside of Texas to the purchaser in Texas, but one part of the soda fountain consisting of a carbonator had been repossessed from a previous purchaser in Texas. It is therefore evident that in the latter two cases, cited above, the Courts of Civil Appeals were of the opinion that the interstate transaction was not destroyed even though part of the united whole consisted of property situated in Texas owned by the foreign corporation. These last three cases show how difficult it is now to determine the exact effect of the decision of the Supreme Court of the United States in the York Manufacturing Company-Colley case. In other words, just what proportion of the property may be purchased by the foreign corporation in Texas before the contract loses its interstate character is difficult to determine. When are the subsidiary promises "relevant and appropriate" to the main interstate contract?

It seems to the writer that the courts in the last three cases cited above reached the correct result. In the Southern Discount

Appellant cites Davis v. United Shoe Repairing Machine Co., Tex. Civ.App., 

92 S.W.2d 1107, as strongly in support of his contention that the dealings between the instant parties are intrastate. As pointed out by Judge 

Combs, the facts in the Davis case were meager. Therein the Massachusetts lessor retained many elements of control over the rented machines not essential to the original transaction of lease, and emphasizes the truism that each case involving commerce, whether interstate or intrastate, must be determined by the facts of the particular controversy. 

So, in the present record, the test to be applied is, whether the so-called service obligation of defendant company was directly relevant and appropriate to the rental and use of these machines. The terms of defendant's contract are simply 'to make good by repair or replacement any imperfections or defects in material or workmanship in said machines for the term herein stipulated; provided said machines shall be properly cared for and properly prepared for elections'; to 'send a representative to the County before the first election at which the machines are to be used, to instruct the persons who will have charge of the machines, so that such persons can properly care for and prepare the machines for elections and can properly instruct the election officers and voters in their use.' Considering the apparently complex mechanism of these voting devices to the uninitiated, their qualities of novelty to recurring sets of electors and officials, we conclude the above local features of the transaction were but incidental and appropriate to the lessors' duty of full performance. All the materials used in building the "producers" were shipped from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to Fort Worth, Texas, by the plaintiff with the exception of one hundred fifty-five dollars of "red brick, sand, lime and cement." It took five weeks to "build" the producers and the labor in Texas cost $917. Therefore, the cost of the materials shipped into Texas and the plaintiff's estimated profits amounted to $4,- 328. As the installation cost such a small percentage of the amount agreed upon for the entire job, if the contract were prepared today, the sales feature of the agreement would be stressed, and it would seem reasonable to provide that the company agrees to install the machinery as incidental to the sale of the "producers." may prescribe certain rules and regulations governing the consignee in his sale of the goods without the courts holding that the corporation is transacting business in this state. "There is. no inconsistency here, for a consignee under any consignment. contract is in an important sense the agent of the owner. The agent or consignee obligates himself to furnish a place of business, to display the goods for sale, and to sell the same, and pay all of the expenses of every sort connected therewith. The business of selling the consigned stock is entirely different and apart from the business of consummating the consignment contract. 

The latter involves the execution of the contract, while the former consists in the performance of its terms. The cases are almost legion to the effect that the business of selling consigned goods does not become that of the owner where he merely limits or regulates the manner, place, time, terms, or details of such sales. Such regulations and limitations do not constitute the control (that) of an owner and operator of the business. Such has been the holding where stipulations were under consideration as follows: Granting exclusive right to purchase and sell goods in a stated territory; requiring a stated stock of goods. to be kept on hand; requiring goods to be located in a particular place or displayed in a particular way, or to be properly cared for; agreement to insure in favor of the owner, or to permit the owner to inspect at will; obligating the purchaser or consignee to keep and send an inventory to the owner on request, not to sell except at fixed prices, not to sell other goods; agreement by the consignee to distribute advertising matter; permitting the consignee to defer payment until goods are resold; requiring purchaser to devote entire time to sale of the goods, or to pay proper attention to sale, or conserve the best interests of the agency, or to use best endeavors to further business or push sales; agreement not to assign agency or remove it."4 If the limitations and regulations are held to be unreasonable so as to give the for- 594. § 1089. Right of Foreign Corporation to Sue 

In the early case of Bank of Augusta v. Earle it was definitely settled by the United States Supreme Court that a corporation could exist outside of the state of its creation by the rules of comity, and that it had the right to sue in the state, by rules of comity, unless it was clearly prohibited by a statute or the policy of the local state. 

The Legislature of the State of Texas has embodied the policy of this state regarding foreign corporations into our statutes." 

These acts require that a foreign corporation wishing to (1) transact business within the state, (2) solicit business within the state, or (3) establish an office within the state, to obtain a permit from the Secretary of State showing a compliance with our statutes.10 As to the right of a foreign corporation to sue, it is provided: "No such corporation can maintain any suit or action either legal or equitable, in any Court in this State upon any demand, whether arising out of contract or tort, unless at the time 5. It goes without saying that the corporation can recover on intrastate transactions created after it obtains a permit. This is true as to the items of a running account contracted after the permit was obtained.17

When the debtor makes a payment to his creditor he has the privilege of directing on which debt the payment must be credited, but if he does not specify how the payment shall be credited, the creditor is free to credit the amount on any debt owed him by the debtor. Therefore, the foreign corporation is privileged to credit the payment made by its debtor on a debt that was created before it received a permit to transact business in Texas, where the debtor did not specify how the payment should be credited, and recover on the amount that was incurred after the permit was issued.18

A foreign corporation is denied the right to sue on any tort or contractual action. If title to property has become vested in the corporation it can sue for the property without having taken out a permit even though title was acquired while the company was transacting business in Texas without a permit. Co. v. Hannon,19 Justice Levy said: "The failure to obtain the required permit before doing business in the state does not forfeit the title to the property or make null and void the purchase of the same.

The consequences of violating the statute imposing conditions upon the right of a foreign corporation to do business in Texas would be the prohibition to maintain ‘any action in any court of this state' upon any demand, arising in contract or tort, through the business so done. The statute does not annex the penalty nor intend that the violation of such statute shall operate to make void and unenforceable contracts and purchases of property made before its conditions were complied with. As expressly stated in the case of S. R. Smythe Company v. Ft. Worth 

Glass & Sand Co., 105 Tex. 8, 142 S.W. 1157: "The law of this state does not render void the contract made and performed in the transaction of business in this state by the foreign corporation without a permit, but only denies such corporation the right to enforce such contract or cause of action arising out thereof (of such transaction) in the courts of this state.'

A foreign corporation may maintain suit on any cause of action arising legally, that is, a judgment taken, or account, or cause of action, arising while the corporation has a permit and before it has surrendered it. FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1090. Effect of Non-Compliance with Conditions-Failure to Se cure a Permit

A foreign corporation transacting intrastate business without securing a permit is subjected to the following statutory penalty: "No such corporation can maintain any suit or action, either legal or equitable, in any court of this State upon any demand, whether arising out of contract or tort, unless at the time such contract was made, or tort committed, the corporation had filed its articles of incorporation under the provisions of this chapter." "' 26 (* In all cases of statutory construction the object is to ascertain the intention of the Legislature, and when the intention is ascertained it must be given effect. The Supreme Court 27 in construing this article said: it is not expressly declared nor necessarily implied that any contract or right which might be entered into or acquired by a foreign corporation without compliance with the statute should be void. The statute expressly denounces (fixes) the penalty against such failure to comply with the law as being barred from the courts of the state to assert any right that such corporation may have growing out of a transaction had without complying with the terms of the said statute.”

In the Metropolitan-Kane case the court said: "Under the law of Indiana, as already determined, the Chicago Trust Company was precluded from maintaining a suit in the courts of that state, and it would follow that plaintiff is likewise precluded.

It does not follow, however, as contended by the defendants, that because the Chicago Trust Company was barred from the courts of Indiana, it was also barred from the Federal courts. Their validity, in our judgment, could not be affected by the fact that the Chicago Trust Company, subsequent to their assignment, ceased to exist as a corporate entity. "A construction of the statutory provisions in question, as precluding a non-complying foreign corporation from suing in the Federal court, would, in our judgment, raise a serious question as to their validity. Nor does such a statute prevent a recovery upon such contract in an action prosecuted in some other state. This would not be true if the contract were void in the state where it was executed. Such contracts are not void, but remain valid and enforceable by suit in the Federal courts or in the courts of any other jurisdiction though there has been no attempt to comply with the statute.' 999

One Court of Civil Appeals in a dictum stated that if a foreign corporation comes to Texas and transacts business without a permit it can not recover on an intrastate transaction in a Texas court, but it can recover in the courts of another state if the court gets jurisdiction of the defendant. However, the Court said that such corporation could not recover judgment in a Texas court on such foreign judgment.42 In this case Justice Talbot said: "The next question is, if appellant's original cause of action did not grow out of a transaction involving interstate commerce, and it had no permit to do business in Texas, was it permissible to show those facts in bar of appellant's right of recovery on its judgment which had been obtained in the state of Missouri, and upon which the suit is predicated? That this question should be answered in the affirmative we think is well settled by the opinion in the case of Wisconsin v. Pelican Ins. Co., 127 U.S. 265, 8 S.Ct. 1370, 32 L.Ed. 239. 

The principle applicable, we think, to the present case, is aptly expressed in the following quotation from that case: "The essential nature and real foundation of a cause of action are not changed by recovering judgment upon it; and the technical rules which regard the original claim as merged in the judgment and the judgment as implying a promise by the defendant to pay it do not preclude a court to which the judgment is presented for affirmative action (while it cannot go behind the judgment for the purpose of examining into the validity of the claim) from ascertaining whether the claim is really one of such a nature that the court is authorized to enforce it.' This doctrine, as we understand, is not affected by the provisions of the Constitution of the United States and the act of Congress by which it is declared, in effect, that 'full faith and credit' shall be given in each state to the records and judicial proceedings of every other state. It is said in the case cited that those provisions establish a rule of evidence, rather than of jurisdiction. It is not a question of whether or not the merits of the claim upon which the judgment has been rendered may be inquired into, but whether, when suit is brought upon such judgment in this state, the 

42. St. Louis Expanded Metal Fireproofing Co. v. Beilharz, Tex.Civ. 

App., 88 S.W. 512. 68

Ch. 

court will inquire into the character of the original cause of action, and, if found to have been one that plaintiff could not have maintained a suit upon in this state in its original form, will deny his right to prosecute a suit upon it in its changed form." This quotation is dictum as it was shown in the Beilharz case that the company had a permit when its cause of action arose. The facts showed that the company changed its name during the ten years' permit. The court held that the permit was valid during the remainder of the ten years' permit although the corporation had legally changed its name.

It was formerly held that every suit by or against a corporation incorporated under a federal statute involved a controversy arising under the laws of the United States, of which the federal courts had jurisdiction where the suit involved more than $3,- 000.43 Therefore, if such a corporation was sued in a Texas court and the amount involved was more than $3,000, the defendant could remove the case to the federal court.44 But a federal act of 

1925 provides that no federal district court shall have jurisdiction of any action on the ground of federal incorporation, unless the United States owns more than one-half of the capital stock.45 

Therefore, if the United States owns more than one-half of the capital stock of a corporation created under a federal statute, the old rule still applies, and the federal courts have jurisdiction because a controversy arising under the laws of the United States is involved.46 As to railroad corporations incorporated by Congress, it is now provided: "No court of the United States shall have jurisdiction of any action or suit by or against any railroad company upon the ground that said railroad company was incor-

surrendered.51 In 1931 the Legislature amended article 1536 52 by adding the following provisions: "If any corporation shall transact intrastate business in Texas without first having obtained a permit such corporation shall forfeit to the 

State of Texas not less than One Hundred Dollars ($100.00) nor more than Five Thousand ($5000.00) Dollars for each month or fraction thereof it shall transact such business without a permit as required hereunder, to be recovered in a suit to be brought by the Attorney General in Travis County, Texas, and the State shall have a lien on all properties of the corporation for said penalties and any corporation may be enjoined by the Attorney General when transacting such business without a permit as required hereunder." It is to be noticed that the amendment does not prohibit the transaction of intrastate business without a permit, but only provides additional penalties for doing so, and thus it is felt that the law with respect to the rights of the parties to a transaction entered into by such a corporation are not affected by the amendment. 

If a literal construction is followed in determining the meaning of article 1536, the property of a foreign corporation transacting business in Texas without a permit could be looted, not only by the directors of the corporation, but by third parties. 

The statute provides that, "No such corporation can maintain any suit or action, either legal or equitable, upon any demand, whether arising out of contract or tort." This question was first presented to the Supreme Court of Texas in the case of Pratt-Hewit Oil Company v. Hewit.53 In that case the Supreme Court held that, though the corporation is denied access to our courts, a stockholder can bring a suit in four cases. In three cases the stockholder institutes the suit for the benefit of the corporation in what is known as a shareholder's bill. In other words, a stockholder may bring a suit for and on behalf of the corporation where the directors have acted (a) fraudulently, (b) 

51. Kingman Texas Implement Co. 

v. Borders, Tex.Civ.App., 156 S. 

W. 614. 

52. R.S.1925, as amended by Acts 

1931, 42nd Leg., p. 264, ch. 158, § 1, Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1536. 

53. 52 S.W.2d 64, 122 Tex. 38. 71

§

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

ultra vires, or (c) negligently, thereby causing injury to the corporation. The stockholder may also bring a suit in his own interest and, in the interest of all other stockholders, where third parties have appropriated or attempted to appropriate to themselves the property of the corporation. According to the above decision in all other cases other than the four cases mentioned above the corporation and the stockholders are without remedy where the foreign corporation has transacted business in Texas without a permit. In the above case the court said: "If this were a suit brought by stockholders, for the benefit of the corporation, on a cause of action in which no breach of trust or ultra vires act or negligent act was charged against the directors of the corporation, then a different situation would be presented. In such a suit the corporation and its stockholders would be in complete harmony. The corporation cannot even control this suit. It is conducted and directed alone by the stockholders. Clearly, a corporation, which has failed to comply with the law of this State in taking out a permit to do business, will not be permitted to evade the statute denying it access to the courts by the simple expedient of clothing itself in the garb of a stockholder. * "" "A complete answer to this proposition is that the statute does not attempt to bar the suit of the stockholders in an action of this nature. The evident purpose of its enactment was to prevent the corporation, or anyone acting for it, from maintaining a suit arising out of the transaction of business in the state without having obtained the permit required by our statutes. In other words, its purpose was to compel corporations to obey the laws of this State in reference to obtaining a permit before transacting business in the State. The corporation is penalized by the State because of its failure to comply with laws regulating the transaction of its business and the act must be so construed as to make it effective for this purpose. It would penalize certain stockhold- 

54. The point was decided by two courts of civil appeals before the

Pratt-Hewit case arose. Favorite 

Oil Co. v. Jef. Chaison Townsite Co., 162 S.W. 423; Canadian Country Club v. Johnson, 176 S.W. 835. 72

Ch. § 1090 

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

ers if the act be so construed as to enable those in charge of the corporation to defraud them. "We are not to be understood as holding that a foreign or domestic corporation may avoid the effect of the statute which denies it the use of the courts while illegally transacting business in this State by merely having a stockholder bring a suit for its benefit. A suit can only be maintained by a stockholder for the benefit of such corporation when the cause of action sought to be asserted falls within one of the three classes which we have described, that is, where the directors are guilty of fraud, ultra vires acts, or negligence resulting in injury to the stockholder. 

If the cause of action sought to be asserted is merely the ordinary one which accrues to the corporation in the due course of its business, it is of course barred from bringing the same, nor can such suit be maintained for its benefit by its agent, assignee, or stockholder. "It will be noted that the statutes regulating the transaction of business by foreign corporations in regard to obtaining a permit, do not, as in some states, make void any transaction entered into by such corporations while illegally transacting business. The law does not attempt to forfeit the property acquired by such corporations while unlawfully doing business in the State. 

Since this is true, when a corporation, domestic or foreign, has been denied the right to use our courts as a penalty for its failure to comply with the laws of this State, the property the corporation holds in trust for its stockholders is not subject to appropriation by third parties. In such cases, the suit must be brought, not for the benefit of the corporation, but by the individual stockholders, suing in their own right. A court of equity, in such case, possesses full power and authority to take such action as is necessary and proper to protect the interests of the stockholders in the corporate property.

From these quotations it is evident that the corporation and the stockholders have no remedy on claims arising out of transacting business in Texas by a foreign corporation without a permit unless it comes within one of the excepted categories. In three cases the stockholder may sue for the corporation even 73

§ 

Ch. 25

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

though the cause of action arose out of the transaction of business in Texas, and no one can appropriate the property of the corporation without being subjected to an individual suit by a stockholder. It would seem that the holding of the court in the first three instances is inconsistent with some of the expressions on the part of the court. For instance, in one of the quotations the court stated that, "The evident purpose of its enactment was to prevent the corporation, or any one acting for it, from maintaining a suit arising out of the transaction of business in the State without having obtained the permit required by our statutes." The plaintiff in the above suit alleged that the directors of the company were attempting to defraud the corporation of some of its property by entering into a collusive lease of the property of the company with another corporation. This transaction certainly arose "out of the transaction of business in the State." 

However, the court held that where the directors acted fraudulently, ultra vires, or negligently, a stockholder could bring what is ordinarily designated as a shareholder's bill. Every shareholder's bill is in substance a suit by and for the corporation. Why the court made these three exceptions to the statute is not selfevident. There is really no authority for the broad statement copied from Cook on Corporations. In effect the result of the decision is that the corporation is given a remedy through a shareholder's bill where the directors have acted fraudulently, ultra vires, or negligently. The shareholders are permitted to recover in an individual suit where the defendant has appropriated some of the assets of the corporation. Suppose, however, that the defendants who are not officers of the corporation with knowledge that the foreign corporation has not taken out a permit in Texas, by the most flagrant fraud acquires the property of the corporation at a very inadequate price. In such case the corporation and the stockholders are without remedy according to the above quotations from the Pratt-Hewit case, since the above wrong was not perpetrated by the directors but by a third party.55 The opinion 

55. In Texas Land & Mortg. Co. v. 

Worsham, 13 S.W. 384, 76 Tex. 566, the court said that the property rights of the corporation would be protected although acquired when the foreign corporation had no permit. 74

Ch. § 1090 

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

in the Pratt-Hewit case is very unsatisfactory and will be modified when put to the test.

As has been stated in a preceding paragraph, a shareholder's bill is in reality a suit by the corporation. As is explained in detail in the chapter on Suits by Shareholders, when the corporation is under the domination of the guilty directors a shareholder is permitted to bring a suit for the corporation where the directors will not bring the suit, but the corporation must be made a defendant and the recovery, when collected, is paid to the corporation. Where the shareholder is permitted to recover in three cases-fraud of the directors, ultra vires, and negligence the corporation is recovering although by the specific terms of our statute it is prohibited from doing so since these causes of action arose out of transacting business in Texas. As soon as the courts of Texas realize that in those three cases the Texas statute is actually repealed by a court decision, they will not blindly follow the dictum in the above decision. When the courts fully sense what peculiar results follow from this dictum, they will refuse to follow it to its logical conclusion. For instance, the court said if the damage is caused by the fraud of the directors, the corporation would be given relief through a shareholder's bill. 

As the directors in the case defrauded the corporation by leasing some of its property to an oil company, the corporation was permitted to recover, although it had never applied for a permit. The court assumed that the statute did not prohibit such a suit because the court said that the Texas legislature could never have intended such a result as the promoters of so many foreign corporations would organize them with the idea of coming to Texas for the purpose of looting them. It would seem more reasonable to say that the Texas legislature intended that exact result so that not many of such corporations would be incorporated as Texas cannot afford to become the dumping ground of directors with so little honor. If some of these corporations are refused recovery, the stockholders will be more careful in the selection of the directors. Why should the court permit recovery where the fraud was perpetrated by the directors and not if by third parties. If the entire property of the corporation is obtained by a 75

§ 

Ch. 25

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

third party through a flagrant fraud while the company is transacting business in Texas, the company is without remedy even though a stockholder brings a shareholder's bill where the directors were not guilty of negligence in permitting the third party to defraud the company. If the fraud was so flagrant as to amount to theft (if such is possible) the court said the shareholders could bring individual suits for the recovery of the loss. 

According to the dictum in the Pratt-Hewit case the company will be permitted to recover through a shareholder's bill if the transaction is ultra vires, but not if intra vires. Therefore, if a foreign mercantile corporation comes to Texas and transacts business without a permit and lends the defendant $2,500 evidenced by his note, the corporation in a Texas court through a shareholder's bill will be permitted to collect the entire amount due, since the transaction is ultra vires. But if a foreign state bank is the lender no recovery will be permitted, since the loan is intra vires. If however, the maker of the note gives the directors $1,- 

000 as a bribe for the surrender of the note very probably the judge that wrote the opinion in the Pratt-Hewit case would either let the corporation recover through a shareholder's bill or the individual stockholders in a personal action. The Commission of Appeals will never be able to reconcile their decisions if they continue to follow the dictum of the Pratt-Hewit case. 

The Texas Supreme Court should say frankly that a shareholder's bill is a suit by the corporation and deny recovery in all of the three cases referred to in the Pratt-Hewit case. According to the dictum in the above case, if anyone steals the property of the foreign corporation, the shareholders are forced to institute an individual suit for their personal damages. In such action the amount of the recovery would depend on the financial condition of the company as reflected in the balance sheet. If the assets of the company equaled its liabilities without putting the amount of the capital stock on the liability side of the balance sheet the shareholders would not recover anything. If that is not the meaning of the above dictum, and if the court meant to say that the shareholders can recover the actual value of the assets converted by the defendant, the holding is so unjust to the creditors 76

Ch. § 1090 

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

of the corporation that no court will follow the decision. Clearly in such case the corporation should recover for the benefit of its creditors if anyone is permitted to maintain the suit. 

By the great weight of authority the corporation is permitted to recover where the defendant has converted some of the property of the corporation to his use and benefit. For this reason it was not necessary for the court to say that the shareholders are the equitable owners of the property of the corporation and, therefore, have a personal action where the property of the corporation is stolen. The statute provides that the corporation cannot recover in a Texas court on causes of action arising out of the transaction of intrastate business. The corporation may have acquired title to the property converted in an interstate transaction or when it had a permit to transact business in Texas. If it acquired title while engaged in an intrastate transaction without a permit, the title vested in the corporation and a suit for the conversion of the property is for interference with the company's title and is not on a cause of action arising out of the transaction of intrastate business. This rule was decided by the Supreme Court of Texas as early as 1890 and has been followed by the Courts of Civil Appeals and many other courts of the American Union.56

Court in McMullen v. Burton, etc., Corporation, 138 S.W.2d 823, was to the same effect. After reviewing the legislative history of the subject, we concluded by saying, in substance, that the Legislature had manifested no purpose to deprive an unregistered corporation of the right to urge any and all available defenses to litigation waged against it, and as the Legislature had not seen fit to do so, clearly a court would not be authorized to add to the penalties prescribed by the Legislature, the additional penalty of depriving a foreign corporation of the valuable right of defending itself in the courts."

Article 52431 of said Revised Statutes, as amended by Laws 1897, p. 168, c. 120, provides that: 'Any corporation, either domestic or foreign, which shall fail to pay the tax provided for in this article at the time specified herein, shall, because of such failure, forfeit its right to do business in this state, which forfeiture shall be consummated, without judicial ascertainment, by the Secretary of State entering upon the margin of the ledger kept in his office relating to such corporations, the word, "forfeited," etc. In neither of these statutes, nor any other, so far as we are advised, is it provided that the certificate of the Secretary of State declaring that the right of a corporation to do business in this state has been forfeited shall be evidence of such forfeiture. 

In the absence of such provisions, it must be held that such certificate is no evidence of that fact. It will be observed that the articles quoted expressly provide that a certified copy of a permit to do business by the Secretary of State shall be evidence of the compliance with the law requiring such permit; and also that a certificate of the Secretary of State that the corporation 80

has failed to file in his office its articles of incorporation shall be evidence that such corporation has in no particular complied with the law. The Legislature having thus restricted the use of the certificate of the Secretary of State as evidence of matters pertaining to his office, the courts are not at liberty to extend the application of such statute to matters not expressly authorized thereby." 

§ 1092. Pleading and Proof of Permit 

Exactly when the plaintiff-foreign corporation must allege and prove that it had a permit to do business in Texas when the cause of action in litigation arose, was not definitely determined by the decisions of the Supreme Court of Texas until recent years. In 

1897 in the case of Taber v. Interstate Building & Loan Ass'n 65 the court intimated that in every suit by a foreign corporation in a Texas court the burden is on the plaintiff to allege and prove a permit unless the petition showed that the cause of action was created in favor of foreign corporations engaged in interstate commerce or such as are employed by the United States in the transaction of its business." By a recent decision by the Commission of Appeals which was adopted by the Supreme Court of Texas, and other cases decided in the last decade, the law has been classified and is now fairly definite and well understood by the Texas lawyers.66

If the petition shows on its face that the foreign corporation is transacting business in the state without the required permit, 65. 40 S.W. 954, 91 Tex. 92.

In Feder v. Texas Bitulithic Co., Tex.Civ.App., 82 S.W.2d 724, Pelphrey, C. J., said: "We have con 

Icluded that we were in error in holding, in our original opinion, that it was not necessary for defendant in error Texas Bitulithic Company to prove that it had a permit to do business in Texas. While it is true that, unless the petition shows that the corporation is doing business in Texas, the fact must be specially pleaded to place upon such corporation the burden of proof as to a permit, yet it is equally true, according to the recent holding of our Commission of

County Lumber Co., 124 Tex. 156, 76 

S.W.2d 505, that, where the petition shows that the corporation has an office in the state, it likewise has the burden of showing the issuance of a permit. The petition in the present case showing the existence of an office in Texas, the burden was on the 

Bitulithic Company to prove that it had been granted a permit to do business in Texas. The record showing that, when the question of the authority to maintain the suit was raised in the trial court, defendants in error's attorney requested a continuance in case the court held the proof necessary, we shall reverse and remand the case rather than dismiss the suit, as would probably be our duty if defendants in error had had an opportunity to prove up their permit."

We think the rule is well settled that a corporation, incorporated under the laws of another state, is required to make the further allegation that, as such, it has a 'permit to do business in the State of Texas' (Chapman v. 

Hallwood Cash Register Co., 32 Tex. 

Civ.App. 76, 73 S.W. 969); and the burden rests upon such corporation to prove the facts so alleged. However, failure to sustain the allegation by proof does not become fundamental error on appeal, unless presented in such manner as to enable an appellate court to consider the error apparent from the record. § 1094. Proof of the Existence of a Permit

1096. Disposition on Appeal 

When an appellate court is called upon to revise the judgment of a trial court, it must do so upon the record before the court when the judgment was rendered. A party to a suit will not be permitted to try his case in the appellate court on a different statement of facts than that presented in the court below. If the petition shows that the plaintiff is a foreign corporation and that the transaction in question is intrastate, then as a condition precedent to a valid judgment, the corporation must both allege and prove that it had a permit to do business in this state when the transaction was created. As Article 1536 16 only prohibits a foreign corporation from suing on contracts and torts, the statute has no application to the question of the liability of a foreign corporation to be sued within the state.17

In Adam V. Saenger, Tex.Civ. 

App., 101 S.W.2d 1046, certiorari denied, 59 S.Ct. 832, 307 U.S. 628, 83

L.Ed. 1511, in discussing when a personal judgment is valid against a foreign corporation Justice O'Quinn said: "But, if we are in error in construing the California statutes above discussed, and it should be said that they do authorize service upon nonresidents in proceedings such as here by service on the lawyer or person representing the nonresident-that is by substituted service, then such statute is without force, because as said in Black on Judgments, 2d Ed., Sec. 904, p. 1343, 'No

State can extend its jurisdiction over a person who is not a resident of such state and not within its limits at the time, and who does not appear or authorize an appearance, so as to render a judgment or decree which shall be binding upon him personally. 

For that purpose, constructive or substituted service is of no avail.' 

The instant suit being one in personam and not in rem, and the judgment being one by default on substituted service on a nonresident defendant must be treated as a nullity in this state which is called upon to enforce it by action. Pennoyer v. Neff, 95 U.S. 714, 725, 727, 24 L.Ed. 565. 

In the cited case, it is said: 'But where the entire object of the action is to determine the personal rights and obligations of the defendants, that is, where the suit is merely in personam, constructive service in this form upon a nonresident is ineffectual for any purpose.' It is well settled that a judgment rendered in one state against a resident of another state, who was not served with process and did not appear in the action, either personally or by authorized attorney, is not valid or binding out of the state where rendered, although the attempt to acquire jurisdiction may have been in a mode recognized as sufficient and valid by the laws of the state where the judgment was rendered; and such absence of jurisdiction will defeat an action on such judgment for its enforcement in any other state. Black on Judgments, 2d Ed., vol. 2, Sec. 

906, p. 1347 (and authorities cited).

The principles of the law relating to the acquisition of jurisdiction by courts over nonresident defendants, apply equally to foreign corporations as to natural persons. A corporation is a resident of the state which creates it, and if sued in the courts of another state, jurisdiction over it can only be acquired in some mode equivalent of personal service of process on an individual."

Texas statute 23 provides that suit may be brought against a private corporation "in any county in which the cause of action or a part thereof arose." This provision is applicable to foreign corporations. The United States Supreme Court held a similar statute in Arkansas unconstitutional on the grounds that it was discriminatory.25 But as the statutes are not identical, the Texas 

Commission of Appeals did not follow the above case but distinguished it from the case before the court 26 on the ground that the Arkansas statute discriminated between domestic and foreign corporations, while the Texas statute applies to both alike.

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1098. Service on Foreign Corporations 

The parties that may be served in order to acquire jurisdiction of a foreign corporation are named in Art. 2031.41 This article as amended by Acts 1919, p. 181, provided: "In suits against a foreign corporation, joint stock company or association, or acting corporation or association, process may be served on the president, vice president, secretary, treasurer, or general manager, and in any cause of action arising within this State, process may also be served upon any local or traveling agent, or traveling salesmen of such corporation, joint stock company or association, or acting corporation or association in this state." 42 By the Acts of 1935, 44th Leg., 2nd C.S., p. 1688, ch. 431, § 1, the above article was amended so as to read as follows: "In any suit against a foreign corporation, joint stock company or association, or acting corporation or association, pending or hereafter filed in this State, to which any foreign corporation is a party or is to be made a party, process may be served on the President, Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer, General Manager, or upon any local or travelling agent or travelling salesman of such corporation, joint stock company or association, or acting corporation or association in this State."

By a recent enactment 48 the legislature has provided that each foreign corporation with a permit to do business in Texas, or that has applied for a permit, must file a power of attorney with the Secretary of State, designating some individual who is a resident of this state, as its agent upon whom process may be served in all suits brought in this state. By express terms this act is made

cumulative of all existing statutes.

This act is published as arti cle 2031a in Vernon's Annotated Civil Statutes. It provides: 

"Sec. 1. From and after the effective date of this Act, each and every foreign corporation seeking a permit to do business in this State, and as a prerequisite to its right to secure a permit to do business in Texas, and each and every foreign corporation already having a permit to do business in this State on the effective date hereof, shall file in the office of the Secretary of State a power of attorney designating some individual who is a resident citizen of this State, as its service agent, upon whom process may be served in all suits, proceedings and causes of actions pending or hereafter filed in this State, in which said foreign corporation is a party or is to be made a party, which power of attorney shall be in effect so long as said foreign corporation is authorized to do business in Texas, and for a period of four years from and after the date any such foreign corporation shall have surrendered its charter or has ceased to do business in Texas; provided, however, that each foreign corporation having a permit and doing business in Texas on the effective date hereof, shall have ninety days after the effective date hereof within which to comply with the requirements of this Act. "Sec. 2. The power of attorney required by this Act shall, in addition to stating the name and address of the agent, also stipulate that said agent is appointed as the corporation's service agent in Texas, and that said foreign corporation consents to the service of process upon said agent and that he shall be deemed as the service agent of said corporation for all intents and purposes as contemplated by the Statutes requiring such designation and appointment; said power of attorney shall be acknowledged by the President or Vice-President, attested by the Secretary and acknowledged in manner and in form as is required in the acknowledgment of deeds in the State of Texas; said power of attorney shall, when executed, be filed in the office of the Secretary of State and shall become a part of the records in said office. "Sec. 3. In the event of the death, resignation or removal of said agent so appointed, or the revocation of said power of attorney by said corporation, said foreign corporation shall imme- 103

§ 

Ch. 25

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS 

diately substitute the name of some other individual by similar power of attorney as is required by this Act, so that at all times an agent shall be available upon whom service of process may be had as provided herein. "Sec. 4. Nothing herein contained shall be construed as repealing any statute in force in this State in reference to service of process on foreign corporations, but this Act shall be construed and held cumulative of all existing statutes, and service of process in all suits against foreign corporations may be had as is now provided by law, or as provided in this Act, or by all of such methods. "Sec. 5. If any corporation which is required by the terms of this Act to file the power of attorney and designate a service agent as provided by this Act, shall fail to do so at or within the time as required by this Act, then in such event: "(a) Each of its acts in this State shall, as to it, be unlawful and void and none of such acts shall, as to it, be valid; and it shall be incapable in this State of receiving the benefit of exercising in its behalf or enjoying any right, power, privilege or immunity that shall not already have accrued, provided that none of its acts done subsequently to the filing of such a power of attorney, though such filing be late, shall be affected by the foregoing provisions, nor in case of such late filing shall the incapacity affected by the foregoing provisions apply to any right, power, privilege or immunity that shall have wholly arisen and accrued after such filing. "(b) Such corporation shall be incapacitated to maintain any suit or legal proceedings in any court in this State upon any demand whether arising out of contract or tort. "(c) Such corporation shall be liable to the State of Texas in the penal sum of Fifty ($50.00) Dollars, per week for each and every week in which it shall have so failed to file any such power of attorney, same to be recoverable by the Attorney General in the name of the State of Texas, in any court of competent jurisdiction in Travis County, Texas.
