§ 1099. Omissions or Defects of Article 2031a 

The act partly cures a defect that has long been felt in Texas, as often it is very difficult to find an agent of a foreign corporation upon whom service may be had. But this recent statute does not go far enough. It provides that the corporation must designate "some individual who is a resident of this State, as its service agent, upon whom process may be served so long as said foreign corporation is authorized to do business in Texas, and for a period of four years from and after the date any such foreign corporation shall have surrendered its charter or has ceased to do business in Texas." Suppose "the designated resident citizen" who is "the service agent" leaves the State soon after the corporation "has ceased to do business in Texas," or dies, how could the Court get jurisdiction of the defendant corporation?

The statute should be amended so as to provide that the Secretary of State will be the "service agent" after the company has withdrawn from Texas. It should provide when the Secretary of State is served he will give notice of such service to the foreign corporation. Even though the statute fails to provide for notice by the Secretary of State the statute would be constitutional for "the power of the State altogether to exclude the corporation, and the consequent ability to condition its entrance into the State, distinguishes this case from those involving substituted service upon individuals, Flexner v. Farson, 248 U.S. 

289, 39 S.Ct. 97, 63 L.Ed. 250; Wuchter v. Pizzutti, 276 U.S. 13, 48 S.Ct. 259, 72 L.Ed. 446, 57 A.L.R. 1230, whose entrance into a

State may render them amenable to action there, only if the statute providing for substituted service incorporates reasonable provision for giving the defendant notice of the initiation of litigation, Hess v. Pawloski, 274 U.S. 352, 47 S.Ct. 632, 71 L.Ed. 

1091. The fact that appellant qualified to do business in the 

State and complied with the registration statute also distinguishes cases of attempted service on a state official pursuant 105

to a statute with which the defendant corporation had never complied, and where at the time of suit it had removed from the state and was transacting no business there." 44

It is true that subdivision (d) of section 5 of the above statute provides for service on the Secretary of State where "such corporation" has failed to appoint a "service agent." But it does not provide for service on the Secretary of State if the local service agent appointed by the corporation dies or leaves the State after the company has withdrawn.45 The amendment applies to corporations "seeking a permit to do business in this state" and "every foreign corporation already having a permit to do business in this state." It does not include corporations that transact intrastate business in Texas without a permit unless they have applied for a permit. Therefore, in that case the Secretary of State does not become the service agent of such foreign corporations. 

As we have seen in a preceding section, if a foreign corporation transacts intrastate business in Texas without a permit, the obligation thereby created in favor of such corporation is not null and void and may be enforced by the corporation in the Federal court if more than three thousand dollars are involved, or in a state court other than Texas if jurisdiction of the defendant is acquired by a court of competent jurisdiction. 

Since Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 2031a is restricted to foreign corporations that (1) are seeking to obtain a permit, and (2) have already secured a permit, a very important question will soon confront the Texas courts. By section 5 of the above statute it is provided that if any corporation which is required by the terms of this Act to file the power of attorney and designate a service agent, shall fail to do so, "each of its acts in this state shall, as to it, be unlawful and void and none of such acts shall, 44. In other words, by the plain terms of the above Act, a foreign corporation that transacts intrastate business in Texas that has either obtained a permit or has applied for a permit, cannot recover on any obligation created in its favor, since such obligation is null and void, if it has not appointed a service agent in accordance with the terms of the statute. 

Our Supreme Court held in the case of State Bank of Chicago v. Holland 46 that under Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1536 before it was amended in 1931 an obligation created in favor of a foreign corporation transacting business in Texas without a permit is not null and void. Then the only penalty was that it could not obtain a judgment in a Texas court on such an obligation. Therefore, it seems that at this time in Texas the same rule would apply to foreign corporations that come to Texas and transact business where the corporation never applies for a permit. However, if the company has a permit or has applied for a permit and does not comply with the above statute, since obligations created in its favor are void, the Supreme Court of Texas may hold that even a note payable to it in the hands of an innocent purchaser is null and void. Judge Phillips in Washer v. Smyer 47 held that an illegal note in the hands of an innocent purchaser is binding on the maker; but if the statute provides that the note is "void," it is unenforceable even in the hands of an innocent purchaser. Therefore, article 2031a should be amended and made applicable not only to corporations (1) that have a permit or (2) that have applied for one, but also to corporations that come to Texas and transact intrastate business without applying for a permit. The statute would not be unconstitutional if it included such corporations as to liability which accrued from transacting business in Texas, since they voluntarily transact business in Texas, and, are therefore "present" in Texas and consent to be bound by our laws.48

FOREIGN CORPORATIONS § 1100. Suit against Foreign Corporation on Causes Arising Out side of Texas

In order to permit transitory actions against foreign corporations in a state other than the corporation's domicile, the states have adopted numerous statutes of various sorts. The usual requirement is that the corporation "do or transact business" in the state in which suit is brought.55 The statutes provide either that service of process may be had upon a local agent, or upon certain corporation officers, or upon an agent designated to receive such service, or upon a certain state official.56 The federal decisions are ultimately controlling in cases arising under these statutes. If service of process is upon an agent designated by the corporation to receive such service, "real consent" to the court's jurisdiction is obtained; but if the service of process is not upon an agent so designated, there is said to be only "implied consent" to the jurisdiction of the court.57 Where the foreign corporation has designated a service agent, in other words where there is "real consent," suit may be had upon causes of action arising out of business done within the state or for causes of action arising from business done without the state, depending upon the terms of the agent's appointment and those of the state statute.58 The tendency is to construe the appointment as not applying to suits arising from business transacted outside of the state.59 In many statutes it is provided that service of process may be had upon a state official in the absence of designation by the corporation of a

589, noted in 14 Tex.).Rev. 418, for a discussion of the requirement of "doing business."

From this review of the Texas statutes it is evident that in serving a foreign corporation the facts should be carefully investigated to determine what agent is to be served. If the foreign corporation has a permit to do business in Texas or has applied for such permit, service may be had in accordance with the provisions of the Act of 1933, now published as Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 2031a, or the Act of 1935 which amended Article 2031 of the Revised Civil Statutes of 1925 and now published as Article 2031 of the Vernon's Annotated Civil Statutes. Arti cle 2031a is not exclusive. As to corporations included in that article, it is specifically provided that "this article shall be construed and held cumulative of all existing statutes." When article 2031a was passed in 1933, article 2031, Revised Statutes of 1925, was in effect. The Supreme Court of Texas has never decided whether article 2031a is "cumulative" only as to old article 2031 as published in the Revised Statutes of 1925 or as to its amendment in 1935, now published as Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 

2031. However, it seems reasonable to conclude that the Legislature intended to make it "cumulative" as to any amendment of article 2031 subsequently enacted. If that conclusion is correct, foreign corporations that have permits and those that have applied for permits may be served under article 2031 or 2031a. 

If the foreign corporation that is sued in Texas has neither applied for nor received a permit to do business in Texas, it must be served in accordance with Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 2031. 

Article 2031 as amended in 1935 provides that "In any suit against a foreign corporation" certain agents may be served. 

And article 2031a provides that "each and every foreign corporation" that has a permit or has applied for a permit must appoint a service agent "upon whom process may be served in all suits." From these provisions it is evident that both of the above articles revive the provision of the statutes before the 1925 revision and are broad enough to include causes of actions torney," etc., is clearly incorrect.

The statute 73 is very broad, and seems to include all suits, whether arising in Texas or in a foreign state against foreign corporations doing business in Texas with a permit or that have applied for a permit. Process may be served upon a general officer, a local agent, an appointed service agent, or upon the Secretary of State. If service of process is upon the appointed service agent, upon a general officer, or upon a local agent, it would seem, in the light of the terms and history of the statute, and in view of the previous Texas decisions, that suit could be had even though the cause of action arose outside of the state.

In some respects the statute is too narrow. As stated in a previous paragraph, it should be extended so as to include foreign corporations transacting business in Texas without applying for a permit. In another respect the statute may be too broad. 

Wherever the plaintiff is a resident of this state and wherever the cause of action arose in this state, no hardship will be imposed on the corporation by allowing suit in this state; and, many times it is likewise true that the allowance of suit in this jurisdiction by a nonresident plaintiff against a foreign corporation for a cause of action arising out of the state may not impose an undue hardship on the defendant corporation. The law on the latter point is not settled by the authorities. A detailed discussion of the cases will be found in Prof. Beale's text on The 

Conflict of Laws, Vol. 1, §§ 881-919, and in section 73, Goodrich on the Conflict of Laws. The Texas cases have sustained jurisdiction in cases arising out of the transacting of business in Texas, and of causes of action arising in a foreign state." miss the suit. Old Wayne Mutual

§ 1101. Meaning of "Local Agent" in the Venue Statute 

The term "local agent" as used in the statute does not mean a state agent, but an agent at a given place or in a definite territory.81 Where service is on the general manager of the foreign tion, if sued in a state court, to remove to the federal court of that district although the plaintiff could not have chosen the federal court at all.

§ 1102. Venue of Foreign Corporations 

Ever since the decision in the case of Southern Pac. Co. v. Denton 86 the Texas lawyers assumed that a corporation was an "inhabitant" or "resident" only in the state where incorporated within the meaning of the federal venue statute, and, therefore, it was assumed that a Texas citizen could not sue a foreign corporation in the federal court in Texas even though the corporation was transacting business in Texas where the basis of jurisdiction was not diversity of citizenship. Of course, it could be sued in the Texas courts, but the foreign corporation would then have the privilege of removing the case to the federal court if the plaintiff sued for more than three thousand dollars, or trying the case in the state court. The venue of cases in the federal courts is found in Section 51 of the Judicial Code, 28 U.S.C.A. § 

112. That section in part provides: no civil suit shall be brought in any district court against any person by any original process or proceeding in any other district than that whereof he is an inhabitant; but where the jurisdiction is founded only on the fact that the action is between citizens of different States, suit shall be brought only in the district of the residence of either the plaintiff or the defendant 66 # 

It is evident from this statute that if the jurisdiction of the federal court is founded only on the ground of diversity of citizenship, the suit may be brought "in the district of the residence of either the plaintiff or the defendant." Until a recent case by the Supreme Court of the United States that Court held that a corporation was a "resident" or "inhabitant" only of the state where incorporated.87 In 1939 in the case of Neirbo Co. v. Beth-

In the opinion he said: "Logically applied, this theory of nonmigration prevented suit in a non-chartering state, for the corporation could not be there. And such was the practice of the circuit courts until the opinion of Chief Justice Waite in Ex parte Schollenberger, displayed metaphor with common sense. The essential difference between the practice which Mr. Justice Nelson initiated at circuit and the decision in Schollenberger's Case was not a matter of technical legal construction, but a way of looking at corporations. Men's minds had become habituated to corporate activities which crossed state lines. The fact that corporations did do business outside their originating bounds made intolerable their immunity from suit in the states of their activities. And so they were required by legislatures to designate agents for service of process in return for the privilege of doing local business. That service upon such an agent, in conformity with a valid state statute, constituted consent to be sued in the federal court and thereby supplanted the immunity as to venue, was the rationale of Schollenberger's Case.” 89

95. This reason has been repeated several times by the Supreme Court of Minnesota. It is also supported by the better reason that the courts of the state of the corporation's origin afford the most appropriate and efficient forum for the adjudication of such rights. Frequently such courts alone possess power adequate to the enforcement of all necessary judgments. The rule rests upon public policy and efficiency rather than on jurisdictional grounds -more on the want of power to enforce orders rather than on jurisdiction to make them."

The assets of the original company were sold to the defendant company who assumed the debts of the old company. The court held that the sale of all the assets of the Delaware company amounted to a liquidation and that the plaintiff could bring her suit in Texas on the debt evidenced by her preferred stock certificates of the Delaware company as that suit did not involve affairs of internal management. The court said that, "Two major reasons influence courts of chancery to refuse to interfere in the management of the internal affairs of a foreign corporation: First, because the rights arising between a corporation and its members out of such management depend upon the laws of the state under which the corporation is organized. Second, the courts of that state afford the most appropriate forum for adjudication upon the relation between the stockholders and the corporation, and frequently such courts alone possess jurisdiction and power adequate to the enforcement of all decrees that justice may require. A third reason sometimes assigned is that commonly neither the officers, the governing body, nor the records of the corporation, are within the reach of the decrees, orders or processes of any except the domiciliary courts.

§ 1141. In General 

In the main, the business world is conducted by six types of business enterprises, by individuals, partnerships, joint-stock companies, "business or Massachusetts trusts," limited partnerships and corporations. In the case of the first three persons and quasi persons the owner of all or a part of the business is individually liable for all the debts incurred in the conduct of the business. His individual property may be levied upon and sold to pay these debts even before the creditor exhausts the property used in the business.1 The partnership, the Massachusetts trust, and joint-stock companies are creations of the common law, but the limited partnership and the corporation must be authorized by the sovereign. In the limited partnership the general partners are individually liable for all the debts of the firm, but the

"These organizations, commonly denominated 'Massachusetts trusts,' originated because of the hostility of some states towards corporations, and due to the desire of those organizing the same to secure some of the advantages that would be secured by incorporating, without incurring the burdens and restrictions resulting therefrom. Due to statutory provisions in Massachusetts, prohibiting corporations from dealing in real property, this type of organization reached its fullest development and most extensive use in that state, but, as will appear, has been adopted for use in many other states. The chief advantages of such organizations, from the standpoint of those desirous of combining their wealth for business purposes, are that until recently, they were, in most states, free from regulation, enjoyed freedom from corporation taxation, and its members enjoyed the freedom from personal liability that is imposed upon partners. This type of organization is nothing more than an attempt to use the old common law trust for the purpose of carrying on business enterprise." 7

Because of the extensive use and development of the business trust in Massachusetts the term "Massachusetts trust" has become co-extensive with the term "business trust." Also the term "common-law trust" is frequently used, emphasizing the fact that the organization is one formed without the aid of a statute.

By way of definition, "in general the term 'Massachusetts trust' is used to denote an unincorporated organization created for

" 8 The cases abound with definitions, but as is usually the case in the law of business relations, general definitions are of little value. Actually what is a Massachusetts trust is a most difficult question in view of the present status of the authorities. From outward appearance the corporation, the joint-stock company and the Massachusetts trust resemble each other greatly. In each there is a fixed amount of capital stock, shares of stock are issued, the value of each share is determined, generally a fictitious name is chosen, and the actual business is carried on by a few men, either a board of directors or trustees. Although designated as a trust, the Massachusetts trust varies considerably from the ordinary private trust. Mr. Katz has said: "The most significant characteristic of the business trust, and the most important distinction between such trusts and the ordinary trusts established by will or inter vivos, lies in the fact that the business trust is organized, not as a means of affecting a gift or transfer, but as a device for profit-making through the combination of capital contributed by a number of investors. In ordinary trusts the settlor is seldom also the sole or principal beneficiary; in business trusts such is almost invariably the case-the trust res consists of property originally contributed by the beneficiaries themselves." 10

Whether the particular organization, association, or unit under scrutiny is a business trust or some other type of organization is generally said to depend upon the instrument creating it.¹¹

In Phillips v. Blatchford, 137 Mass.

The court assumed, without any discussion, that the association was a partnership.

In Mayo v. Moritz, 24 N.E. 1083, 151 Mass. 481 (1890), property was conveyed to trustees who were given the right to carry on the business without any interference by the stockholders and the trustees were given the right to fill all vacancies. 

The court held that the organization was a "pure trust." 

In Hussey v. Arnold, 70 N.E. 87, 185 Mass. 202 (1904), the shareholders reserved the right (1) to remove trustees and appoint others, (2) to fill vacancies, and (3) to terminate the trust. At this time the Massachusetts Supreme Court would have no hesitancy in declaring that the association was perfectly legal and in deciding that the shareholders were partners. But in the opinion prepared in 1904 the court said: "The agreement creating the trust has peculiar provisions. The object of it apparently was to obtain for the associates most of the advantages belonging to corporations without the authority of any legislative act and with freedom from the restrictions and regulations imposed by law upon corporations. "We have already said that the subscribers were not to be liable to third persons and it would seem 139

§ 

Ch. 26

 "The difference between Hoadley v. County Commissioners, 

105 Mass. 519 (involving the same indenture as that in Gleason v. McKay, 134 Mass. 419), Whitman v. Porter, 107 Mass. 552, Phillips v. Blatchford, 137 Mass. 510, Ricker v. American Loan & 

Trust Co., 140 Mass. 346, 5 N.E. 284, and Williams v. Boston, 208 

Mass. 497, 94 N.E. 808, on the one hand, and Mayo v. Moritz, 151 Mass. 481, 24 N.E. 1083, on the other hand, lies in the fact that in the former cases the certificate holders are associated together by the terms of the 'trust' and are the principals whose instructions are to be obeyed by their agent who for their convenience holds the legal title to their property. The property is their property. They are the masters. While in Mayo v. Moritz on the other hand there is no association between the certificate holders. The property is the property of the trustees and the trustees are the masters. All that the certificate holders in Mayo v. Moritz had was a right to have the property managed by the trustees for their benefit. They had no right to manage it themselves nor to instruct the trustees how to manage it for them. "This brings us to the question of the character of the Boston Personal Property Trust. It is plain that it is a trust and not a partnership. By the terms of the indenture of trust the property contributed by the certificate holders, or that bought with money contributed by them (the original trust property could be acquired in both ways by the terms of the indenture of trust), was to be held by the trustees in trust to pay the income to the holders of the certificates, and on the termination of the trust to divide the trust fund or the proceeds thereof among them. The certificate holders, are throughout called 'cestuis que trustent.' therefore that the business of the trust was intended to be done in a way that would not give anyone dealing with it a right to bring an action at law against anybody, to enforce any contract or liability of the association. "We do not attempt to determine whether all the provisions of this agreement are enforcible in the courts or whether there are such considerations of public policy involved in an attempt of this kind to do business without a legal liability of anybody for debts incurred by the trustees as to merit consideration by the legislature." 

The control in Williams v. Milton is such as referred to by Mr. Rowley as negative control. 26 Mich.L. 

Rev. 290. 140

The certificate holders, or 'cestuis que trustent,' are in no way associated together, nor is there any provision in the indenture of trust for any meeting to be held by them. The only act which (under the trust indenture) they can do is to consent to an alteration or amendment of the trust created by the indenture or to a termination of it before the time fixed in the deed. But they cannot force the trustees to make such alteration, amendment or termination. It is for the trustees to decide whether they will do any one of these things. All that the certificate holders or 'cestuis que trustent' can do is to give or withhold their consent to the trustees taking such action. And the giving or withholding of consent by the cestuis que trust is not to be had in a meeting, but is to be given by them individually. As we have said, no meeting of the cestuis que trust for that or any other purpose is provided for in the trust indenture. The trustees of the Boston 

Personal Property Trust have a right to sell the trust securities and reinvest the proceeds, and also a limited power to borrow on the security of the trust property. The certificate holders, or "cestuis que trustent," as they are called in the trust deed, have a common interest in precisely the same sense that the members of a class of life tenants (among whom the income of a trust fund is to be distributed) have a common interest, but they are not socii, and it is the trustees, not the certificate holders, who are the masters of the trust property. The sole right of the cestuis que trust is to have the property administered in their interest by the trustees, who are the masters, to receive income while the trust lasts, and their share of the corpus when the trust comes to an end.

In the above case the court stressed unduly the fact that in the declaration of trust of the Boston Personal Property Trust there was no provision for "association among the certificate holders nor meeting of the cestuis que trust." For it is evident that no court would hold that the association is a joint stock company merely because the trust indenture reserves the right to the stockholders; for instance, to meet once a year to receive the dividend that may be declared by the trustees or to inspect the books of the association or to do any other thing that does not confer 141

§

upon the beneficiaries the power to control or direct the trustees in managing the affairs of the association. The fact that the shareholders are permitted "to meet", standing alone, should be considered very slight, if any, evidence of control by the shareholders.15 However, some of the writers on this subject have fallen into the same error as did the Massachusetts court in Williams v. Milton. They intimate that some control may be reserved by the shareholders individually and yet the association be held to be a pure trust whereas if the same control is retained by the shareholders as socii the beneficial owners are partners.16

"Whether or not an association is a trust or partnership depends upon the instrument creating it. 

The test is the power of control of the management of the association. If the certificate holders have the power of control, the association is a partnership; if they have not, and the power of control is in the trustees, it is a trust. *

While the primary emphasis is placed upon the element of control, the court at least gives lip service to the requirement of association. It is submitted that the courts in making such statements are not thinking so much of the idea that there must be no provision for meeting of the beneficiaries if there is to be a pure trust as they are thinking of the almost universal requirement of voluntary association as one of the necessary elements of a partnership.

J., said: "But supposing that this was such a business as is mentioned in the act, were the certificate holders the persons to carry it on? It seems to me that they certainly were not. I take it that the persons called trustees in the deed are clearly trustees as distinguished from agents and from directors. The distinction has been pointed out by my Lord, and I entirely agree with it. 

If, indeed, although they were called trustees, the duties which they had to perform were really those of directors, then, although they were called trustees, the legal effect of the deed would be that they would be directors, and if they are directors they are agents; but here it seems to me clear that according to the true construction of the deed they were not directors or agents, but trustees. If that be so, the certificate holders, even if they were associated at all, were not associated for carrying on the business. It was not their business. They could not have been made liable for any contract made by the trustees. It was of course urged that they would be liable as undisclosed principals. But that assumes that the persons who made the contracts upon which they are to be liable are their agents authorized to bind them by their contracts, which is obviously not true. Therefore, even if there be here a business within the meaning of the section, yet it is not carried on by the certificate holders, who are of a larger number than twenty, but by the trustees, who are not of the number of twenty or more; and therefore in either view the case is not within the statute." 

Cotton, L. J., said: "But, in my opinion, what must be shown is that the association by themselves or by their agents carry on a business. Now, here, how can that be said? That the certifi- 150

cate holders do it by themselves can, I think, hardly be contended. All the power which the subscribers of this money had was to attend sometimes at meetings, and the meetings which were held most usually are those mentioned in Clause 26. The only business done at them was to receive and consider a report from the trustees on the condition and affairs of the trust, to appoint auditors to audit the accounts, and to elect new trustees to fill vacancies. It is impossible, in my opinion, to say that the certificate holders are by themselves in any way carrying on any business by reason of what is done at these meetings. 

Then, can it be said that they carry on a business by their agents? In my opinion that cannot be maintained. The trustees here are the only persons who are dealing with the investments, and they are dealing, not as agents for some principal, but as trustees in whom the property and the management of it are vested, and who have the power of changing the investments and securities." James, L. J., was the only one of the judges of the Court of

In conducting the business the trustees incurred the obligation that was the basis of plaintiff's suit. The defendants were two of the creditors who entered into the above arrangement and the plaintiff contended that all of the parties who signed the agreement became partners. The House of Lords held that the creditors of the Smiths were not liable at law as partners for the obligations incurred by the trustees in conducting the business. Most commentators on the effect of this decision, after stating that the House of Lords held that there was no partnership, go further and say that the Lords held "that the arrangement constituted a true trust" and intimate that the Lords held that the creditors were the cestuis que trust.34 There is no suggestion to that effect in the opinions of the Lords, and the writer does not believe that they meant to hold that the non-trustee creditors were cestuis que trust. The real status of the parties under the deed was that the Smiths were the only persons that anyone could contend were the cestuis que trust and the creditors were disclosed agents to whom the Smiths had given an irrevocable "power coupled with an interest" to act for them in determining (1) when the relationship between the Smiths and the trustees should terminate and (2) to establish rules for the conduct of the business carried on by the trustees. If this is true the non-trustee creditors would not be liable for the debts incurred by the trustees of the Smiths under the doctrine of Hardoon v. Bellilios.35 If the

But there is no intimation to this effect in any of the opinions. 

The only point decided was that the creditors were not liable at law as partners for the debts incurred by the trustees. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the Lords decided that the arrangement entered into in this case formed a "business trust." If the conclusion that the creditors were agents of the Smiths is correct, it could be argued that the Smiths reserved the right through their agents (1) to terminate the trust, and (2) to make rules for conducting the business and therefore under the Massachusetts test the court should have held that the trustees and the Smiths were partners. But whether the Smiths and the trustees were partners or stood in the relation to each other of trustees and cestuis que trust was not involved in the case as the Smiths were not parties to the suit. Cox and Wheatcroft were the only defendants in the case, and the sole issue involved was to determine the relation between the trustees and the other creditors. If the Smiths had been made parties to a bill in equity undoubtedly the House of Lords would have applied the rule set forth in Hardoon v. Bellilios as to their liability, if the Lords concluded that a pure trust was formed between the trustees and the Smiths. The Lords would have exempted the non-trustee creditors on the ground that the latter did what they were authorized to do solely as the disclosed agents of the Smiths; and, therefore, would have held that these creditors were not liable for the debts of the trustees. Lord Cranworth must have had this in mind when he said: "The debtor is still the person solely interested in the profits, save only that he has mortgaged them to his creditors. He receives the benefit of the profits as they accrue, though he has precluded himself from applying them to any other purpose than the discharge of his debts. The trade is not carried on by or on account of the creditors; though their consent is necessary in

such a case, for without it all the property might be seized by them in execution. But the trade still remains the trade of the debtor or his trustees; the debtor or the trustees are the persons by or on behalf of whom it is carried on. 

These powers do not appear to me to alter the case. The creditors might, by process of law, have obtained possession of the whole of the property. By the earlier provisions of the deed, they consented to abandon that right, and to allow the trade to be carried on by the trustees. The effect of these powers is only to qualify their consent. They stipulate for a right to withdraw it altogether; or, if not, then to impose terms as to the mode in which the trusts to which they had agreed should be executed; I do not think that this alters the legal condition of the creditors. 

The trade did not become a trade carried on or for them as principals, because they might have insisted on taking possession of the stock, and so compelling the abandonment of the trade, or because they might have prescribed terms on which alone it should be continued. Any trustee might have refused to act if he considered the terms prescribed by the creditors to be objectionable. Suppose the deed had stipulated, not that the creditors. might order the discontinuance of the trade, or impose terms as to its management, but that some third person might do so, if, on inspecting the accounts, he should deem it advisable, it could not be contended that this would make the creditors partners, if they were not so already; and I can see no difference between stipulating for such a power to be reserved to a third person, and reserving it to themselves." 

Lord Wensleydale said: "Can we then collect from the trust deed that each of the subscribing creditors is a partner with the trustees and by the mere signature of the deed constitutes them his agents for carrying on the business on the account of himself and the rest of the creditors? I think not. It is true that by this deed the creditors will gain an advantage by the trustees carrying on the trade; for if it is profitable, they may get their debts paid; but this is not that sharing of profits which constitutes the relation of principal, agent, and partner. 154

"If a creditor were to agree with his debtor to give the latter time to pay his debt till he got money enough out of his trade to pay it, I think no one could reasonably contend that he thereby made him his agent to contract debts in the way of his trade; nor do I think that it would make any difference that he stipulated that the debtor should pay the debt out of the profits of the trade.

The trustees are certainly liable, because they actually contract by their undoubted agent; but the creditors are not, because the trustees are not their agents." 37

Hickman the deed of settlement provided that the creditors "were to accept the provisions for payment of the debts in full satisfaction of their respective claims upon the said Smith & Son," and that if the creditors broke their covenant not to sue, the Smiths "might plead those presents as a general release" but that when the creditors were paid the property should be returned to the Smiths (Hickman v. 

Cox, 18 C.B. 626). These provisions, as stated by Lord Cranworth, gave the creditors "a mortgage" on the property of the Smiths and power to direct the trustees to sell it for the purpose of paying the obligations due the creditors by the Smiths. This shows that the matter falls clearly within Huffcut's definition of "a power coupled with an interest." In defining "a power coupled with an interest," Mr. Huffcut says: "There must be first an interest or title in the thing constituting the subjectmatter of the agency and then, coupled with this, a power to dispose of or otherwise control the thing for the purpose of protecting the interest. 

* * The American rule seems to be that an interest in the subject-matter of the agency by way of security or indemnity, coupled with a power to sell or otherwise dispose of the property, renders the power irrevocable.

The English rule is somewhat broader and is to the effect that where an agreement is given for the purpose of securing some benefit to the donee of the authority (as in the proceeds by way of payment of a debt), such Huff- an authority is irrevocable." cut on Agency, 2nd Ed., pp. 88-89. 

If A owes B $10,000 and B agrees to extend the debt until A can pay him either from the profits of his business or from the sale of the property used in the business, no one will contend that under this agreement B is liable for the debts if he demanded as a condition of the extension of the obligation that A consult and advise with B's attorney in carrying on the business. Likewise, no court should hold that the creditors in Cox v. Hickman are liable for the debts of the trustees because they demanded as a condition for the extension and surrender of their claims that they be appointed the agents of the Smiths with power to determine how the business should be conducted and when it should be wound up. If the business proved successful the creditors would receive an incidental benefit but no more than they were legally entitled to because the agreement provided that the business should be returned to the Smiths as soon as the debts 155

It, therefore, seems evident that there is no justification for saying "that the House of Lords Case of Cox v. Hickman upheld a trust which could not possibly have withstood the test of Williams v. Milton." 38 Nor is the statement that in America "our judges have not been willing to go as far as the English courts," warranted by the two English cases of Cox v. Hickman, and 

Smith v. Anderson. For, as has been shown, the House of Lords in Cox v. Hickman did not decide that the agreement involved in that case formed a pure trust. Under the Massachusetts test a business trust was formed by the declaration of trust involved in Smith v. Anderson, as the only power reserved by the shareholders was "to appoint new trustees to fill vacancies." Even though the shareholders reserve the power "to fill vacancies" among the trustees when one dies, resigns or is removed by a court of equity, the trustees may "act as principals and be free were paid. Any other holding would be, as stated by Mr. Justice Wightman, "unjust and absurd, and so much at variance with natural justice." 8 H.L.C. 298, 299. The creditors "are interested indirectly, as creditors, and not directly, as proprietors." Wells-Stone Mercantile Co. v. Grover, 75 N.W. 911, 7 N.D. 460, 41 L.R.A. 252. In this case the facts are the same as in Cox v. Hickman, except the creditors did not reserve the right to terminate the business or direct how it should be conduct ed. Each particular case is a separate consideration, and as Mr. Magruder has aptly phrased it, "the decision as to the effect of any particular reserved power in the shareholders is not foreordained in the legal nature of things, but will depend chiefly on whether the court looks upon the business trust device with benevolent or hostile eyes; and whichever way the decision goes, respectable legal analogy will be available to sustain the result." 47 It is universally recognized that a reservation to the shareholders of a right to direct the trustees in the management of the business constitutes the organization a partnership and not a trust.48 Similarly, where complete control is in the trustees and the shareholders have only such rights as are incidental to their position as cestuis que trust, to receive a share of the profits, have the trustees removed for misconduct, and receive a share of the corpus upon the termination of the trust, the organization is a pure trust and the shareholders in some states are free from individual liability.49 But other than these two clear-cut cases there is much uncertainty in the authorities. 

The decided cases give us little help in determining what factors really determine the essentials of a business trust. One or more of the following provisions are found in most attempts to form a pure Massachusetts trust: (1) the power to fill vacancies, (2) the power to remove the trustees, (3) the power to elect the trustees periodically, (4) the power to terminate the trust prematurely, and (5) the power to alter or amend the declaration of trust. These factors have significance only when considered in connection with the approved test which most courts seem to follow. An approximation of that test may be stated as follows:

If by the declaration of trust the shareholders reserve the actual or potential power, as a practical matter, to control the trustees in conducting the business of the organization, it is a partnership. But, on the other hand, if the trustees are the principals and not subject, as a practical matter, to the actual or potential control of the shareholders, the organization is a pure trust, and not a joint-stock company.50

Taken in this light the power to fill vacancies in the board of trustees caused by death, resignation, or from any other cause is such an insignificant factor that few, if any, courts would hold that such a reservation alone makes the association a joint-stock company.51 Whether the power to elect trustees at stated intervals creates a joint-stock company rather than a pure trust is not determined by the authorities. Undoubtedly if the power were to elect new trustees every week or every month there would be such control in the shareholders as to make the association a joint-stock company. It would be as reasonable to argue that the stockholders in a corporation are personally liable to its creditors because the stockholders have the latent power to terminate the corporation and to continue the business thereafter as partners. 

No doubt the argument would be made that with powers such as these the shareholders in a business trust have substantially the control over the business that they would have in the ordinary unincorporated joint stock company, where the shareholders could elect a board of managers or directors and had the power to amend the memorandum of association; and that to exempt them from liability in the former case, when they are liable in the latter is to sacrifice substance for form. But there is an important difference, in that in the business trust the personal liability of the trustee is the creditor's guarantee, whereas in the joint stock company the board of managers are simply agents of the shareholders. Hence, resort to the business trust device is not a mere subterfuge or evasion." 60

In Texas, from the earliest times, the private trust has been recognized as a valid, legal relation,62 and nowhere before 1925 was there an intimation that it is opposed to public policy. Even the spendthrift trust has been adopted to its fullest extent by our courts.63 But the law applicable to the business or Massachusetts trust was extremely unsettled in Texas prior to 1925. In that year the Supreme Court of Texas decided the important case of Thompson v. Schmitt 65 which apparently settled the Texas law and closed the door to the business trust as a form of business organization in Texas. The declaration of trust in the instant case provided that the business of the association was to be conducted by named trustees and their successors, in whom was vested the title to all the property, in trust for the holders of the certificates of beneficial interest. The articles expressly granted to the trustees complete power and authority to conduct the business. To the certificate holders was granted only, (1) the right to inspect an accurate record of all receipts and disbursements to be kept by the trustees, (2) the right to receive dividends, (3) on termination of the association the right to have a division of principal and accumulated profits in the trustees' hands, and (4)

But was the court justified in reaching this conclusion where the facts show conclusively that the title to all the property of the trust was vested in the trustees, and the stockholders reserved not a vestige of control over them? Should the court not have said that the trust instrument formed the relation of trustee and cestui que trust, and on this basis determined the rights of the creditor? 66 The court defines an agent as "one who acts in my behalf, for my advantage, and by my authority." Under this definition it is obvious that every independent contractor and every trustee would be an agent, and the court's assumption in the light of its definition would not be incorrect, but this definition of an agent stands alone and is certainly unsatisfactory.

By this construction the court seems to hold that by reason of our limited partnership and corporation statutes the Legislature repealed by implication all rules of the common law which permit one to be interested in a business without being liable for its obligations. The writer has examined very carefully the Journals of the House and Senate of both the First and Twelfth Legislatures and finds that no such intent was in the mind of any legislator. It is evident from the language of these documents that the Legislature passed the limited partnership act and the general incorporation statute for the purpose of granting a privilege to our citizens, for the purpose of putting them on an equality with the inhabitants of other states, and especially to save the time of the Legislature in considering and passing private incorporation acts. There was not the remotest intention on the part of any legislator to repeal by implication any of the common law rules applying to the relation of trustee and cestui. Whether the resulting organization is a simple partnership or a joint-stock company is of little importance today in respect to the technicalities of suing and being sued, since Rule 18 of the new Court Rules, adopted by the Supreme Court of Texas in 1941, gives the partnership and any other unincorporated association the capacity to sue and be sued in the common or assumed name.

§ 1142. Liability of the Trustees, Property, and Shareholders of a 

Massachusetts Trust

In the preceding sections the writer discussed the essentials of a pure Massachusetts trust, showing that the primary emphasis has been placed upon the amount and degree of control reserved by the shareholders in determining whether the organization under observation is a pure trust or a joint-stock company. It is the purpose of the following sections to discuss the liability of (1) the trustees, (2) the trust property and (3) the shareholders (or cestuis que trust) of a pure Massachusetts trust. 

§ 1143. Liability of the Trustees

obligations incurred by them or their agents in conducting the business of the trust. On these obligations the trustees may be sued at law and the executions levied upon their individual property. The reason for this rule of law is clearly stated in Taylor v. Davis 88 as follows: "A trustee is not an agent. An agent represents and acts for his principal, he may be either a natural or artificial person. A trustee may be defined generally as a person in whom some estate, interest, or power in or affecting property is vested for the benefit of another. When an agent contracts in the name of his principal, the principal contracts and is bound, but the agent is not. When a trustee contracts as such, unless he is bound no one is bound, for he has no principal. The trust estate cannot promise; the contract is therefore the personal undertaking of the trustee."

The Michigan Supreme Court in McGovern v. Bennett,89 wherein the plaintiff sued the defendant trustee for commission, expressed the same principle as follows: "The relation of principal and agent does not exist between those interested in a trust and the trustee. The slightest reflection will make it clear that in such cases no authority to act as an agent is ever given. It follows that defendant by contracting as trustee contracted as principal, and made himself personally liable. * * 

One who contracts as principal cannot escape liability by proving that he was acting as an agent." In Connally v. Lyons,90 M. A. T. Con-

Connally died, the court appointed Nathan Connally (a brother of M. A. T. Connally) as trustee of the estate. There was no right of control whatever reserved in the instrument executed by M. A. T. Connally to her father C. 

P. Connally, as trustee, either for herself or for the beneficiaries as such. A test of partnership is the right of control over the property or profits, or to make disposition thereof. (Citing 1 

Bates on Partnership, Section 37.) There was no right whatever in the brothers of the grantor, who were beneficiaries therein, either to control or withdraw their several interest. "But whether or not the trustee of a voluntary association, or a trust estate, is personally liable has not been before our Supreme Court in any case that we can find. That such trustees should be held personally liable is reasonable, because they have in their own hands the means wherewith to reimburse themselves, and should not assume a debt for the benefit of an estate of which they have the sole management and control without prospect of funds for payment thereof. If this principle needed to be enforced by way of illustration, it may be done by the fact that the defendant a few days before the attachment withdrew from the bank the deposit of Connally & Co., amounting to over $4,000 in cash. In Hill on Trustees, Section 588, the doctrine 173

§ 

Ch. 26

is broadly stated that "a trustee who carries on any trade with the trust assets for the benefit of the cestuis que trust will be responsible to the creditors, not only to the extent of the trust assets, but also with the whole of his own property, and he may be made bankrupt and proceeded against in the same manner as any other trader. And it is immaterial that the trade is carried on by him in consequence of an express direction in the trust instrument; although the trust property will doubtless be primarily liable to the creditors, and will be first applied so far as it will go in discharge of liabilities." Purchases by trustees when made in obedience to the trust impose upon them a personal liability; the seller must look to them for payment, and they must look to the trust estate for reimbursement. The court held the defendants individually liable, and said: "The cases are not altogether uniform and consistent, but the rule sustained by the great preponderance of authority is, that if a trustee, guardian, executor, or administrator signs a contract, and merely appends to his signature the title designating his representative capacity, without restricting by the use of apt words his liability to his representative capacity, he is liable on the contract individually. "Although it has sometimes been stated as a reason why the trustee is held personally liable upon his contracts as trustee, is because he has no power to bind the trust estate, he being likened to an agent who has exceeded his authority, we think the true reason why he is held personally liable upon such contracts is, that he has no principal, or, rather, he is the principal himself. The contract is, therefore, necessarily his, and his alone."

In the declaration of trust involved in Thompson v. Schmitt,18 we find the following nugatory and contradictory provisions: "But the holders of said certificates shall not at any time be personally or individually liable for the payment of any indebtedness incurred by the trustees hereunder, nor for the performance of any obligations entered into by the trustees hereunder, nor for the torts of the trustees and for the trust estate or their or its officers, agents, or employees. The trustees hereunder shall not at any time be personally or individually liable for the payment of an indebtedness incurred by them hereunder, nor for the performance of any obligations entered into by the trustees hereunder, nor for the torts of the officers, agents or employees of this trust estate or the trustees. And the trustees shall, in each case in executing notes, deeds of conveyance, or other instruments of writing of any character, specially stipulate that neither the holders of said certificates nor said trustees shall at any time be held personally or individually liable. "Finally, the trustees hereunder may, with reference to the trust property, and the management, leasing, making sale and disposition thereof, do any and every thing that any other owner of similar property whether real or personal, would have the right and power to do."

Clearly the provision that the trustees shall not be liable for their own torts, nor those of their agents, is nugatory. The same is true with reference to the provision that "the trustees shall not be personally liable for an indebtedness incurred by them,” unless a limiting clause is inserted in the contract.14 And most of the above provisions contradict the last one to the effect that “the trustees may do any and every thing that any other owners would have the right and power to do." After the court deterthe fund. But the parties with whom he dealt can hold him personally liable, whatever his situation as regards the trust estate. The fact that they knew of the trust and that he was dealing on its account, will not protect him. He could relieve himself from personal liability only by a definite understanding that the transactions were had upon some other responsibility." 

13. 274 S.W. 554, 115 Tex. 53. 14. 

Betts v. Hackathorn, 252 S.W. 

602, 159 Ark. 621, 31 A.L.R. 847. 182

mines what provisions of the declaration of trust are void or nugatory, its principal task is to determine whether or not, in view of what the trustees did and the provisions of the declaration of trust, the trustees have the right to exoneration or indemnity. 

As we shall see, if the trustees violate the express or implied provisions of the declaration of trust they lose the right to indemnity and exoneration.

Whether the creditor has notice, or not, of the provisions of the declaration of trust should have little to do with the liability of the shareholders so far as the right of unsecured creditors are concerned, and in the absence of the rights of innocent purchasers or mortgagees. If A gives credit to the "Austin Mercantile 

Co." whether or not he knows it is (1) a corporation, (2) joint stock company, (3) a partnership or (4) a business trust, the law determines who is liable and to what extent. If the principal in contracting the obligation acts through an agent the third party is bound by known limitations of the agent's authority. But if the principal acts in person he is not incapacitated from entering into the obligation merely because he has agreed with a third party not to do so. In the case of the business trust, since the trustees are principals, they have the power, though not the right so far as the shareholders are concerned, to violate the provisions of the declaration of trust. And as the creditors work out their rights against the shareholders through those of the trustees and as the rights of the latter are determined by the provisions of the declaration of trust, knowledge, or want of knowledge, on the part of the creditor has little to do with the determination of his rights. The trustees have notice of the provisions of the declaration of trust, and the law determines their rights from what they do and from the provisions of the declaration of trust. 

The declaration of trust is usually recorded in the county where the company does most of its business. A creditor's rights against the stockholders are derivative, and are worked out through the rights of the trustees, even though under local statutes the creditor may have constructive notice of the declaration of trust. But this has little, if anything, to do with determining the obligation of the stockholders. If the creditor, however, has 183

§ Ch. 23 

actual knowledge of the provisions of the declaration of trust, and he and the trustees knowingly attempt to wrong or defraud the shareholders, the courts should hold the obligation illegal, as any contract which violates the duties of a fiduciary is against public policy. In the absence of actual knowledge, the creditor should be allowed to assume that the trustees are acting honestly, and not violating any of the provisions of the declaration of trust. As a matter of fact, in a majority of cases, the creditor does not have actual knowledge of the provisions of the declaration of trust when he deals with the company. If the issue before the court is to determine whether the shareholders have "waived" a provision of the declaration of trust, or whether they are estopped to insist on one or more of these provisions, knowledge on the part of the creditor would, under many circumstances, be material. Take, for instance, the above provision to the effect that the trustees must limit the liability of the shareholders in every obligation they create. It is impracticable to conduct the business of the trust without violating this provision, because (1) in most cases, the trustees neglect to insert the limiting stipulation in obligations incurred by them, and (2) most persons refuse to deal with the trustees if the provision is insisted upon. 

Suppose that, for the above reasons, the trustees and shareholders agree "to waive" the clause, or suppose before the obligation is created the trustees and shareholders assure the creditors that they have "waived" the above provision. In both instances the creditors' rights should be the same as if the provision had never been inserted in the declaration of trust.15

The reader, of course, will understand that it is not contended that the solution of this difficult problem suggested above, has been adopted by the courts. In fact, in Betts v. Hackathorn,16 the Supreme Court of Arkansas held that the shareholders are not liable at law for any of the debts incurred by the trustees if the company is a pure trust. It is not clear from the opinion whether the court based its opinion on the general proposition that in no case are the shareholders in a pure trust liable for the 

15. Burdick on Partnership, pp. 40, 41 (3d Ed.), and cases cited. 

16. 252 S.W. 602, 159 Ark. 621, 31 A. 

L.R. 847. 184

debts created by the trustees in carrying on the business of the trust because the trustees are principals and not agents of the shareholders, or because there was a provision in the declaration of trust limiting the liability of the shareholders. In this case the plaintiff sued the trustees and two shareholders (named Simms and Kinser) in debt for goods sold, alleging that the defendants were partners. By the declaration of trust the trustees were made absolute masters of the business and no authority was conferred upon the shareholders. The court, therefore, properly held that the company was a pure trust.17 And as the plaintiff did not allege any grounds for equitable relief against the shareholders the court properly held that the two shareholders were not liable at law. Had the plaintiff alleged either (1) that the trustees were insolvent, or (2) non-residents, and asked to be subrogated to the rights of the trustees, the court necessarily would have decided whether the trustees had the right to indemnity or exoneration against the trust property and the shareholders individually. The provisions of the declaration of trust in this case are strikingly similar to those quoted above from Thompson v. Schmitt. By paragraph 21 of the declaration it was provided that "every act done, power exercised, or obligation assumed by the trustees shall be done as trustees and not as individuals and that every creditor shall look only to the funds of the trust for payment of any debt, and neither the trustees nor the shareholders, present or future, shall be personally liable therefor"; by paragraph 9 that the "trustees shall have and exercise the exclusive management and control of the same, in any manner that they shall deem fit for the best interest of the shareholders, with all the rights and powers of absolute owners thereof," and by paragraph 20 that "the shareholders shall not be liable for any assessment, and the trustees shall have no power to bind the shareholders personally." The court held that the provision exempting the trustees from personal liability was void. 

The court said: "A general rule in the law of trusts is that a trustee is a principal and not an agent for the cestui que trust. It follows from 

17. See § 1141. 185

§ 

Ch. 26

this rule that the trustee and not the cestui que trust is personally responsible for an indebtedness growing out of transactions in relation to the trust estate. The creditor's guarantee is the personal liability of the trustee. We see no-reason why the trustees here should be exempt from this general rule. Their declaration exempting them from personal liability cannot prevent individual liability from attaching as the law fixes the liability of trustees. 

"The trustees under the terms of the indenture interposed themselves as a shield between the stockholders and creditors, and for that reason are individually liable. "The declaration not only exempts the shareholders from individual liability in specific terms, but shears them of all control and management of the business. Paragraph 9 of the indenture makes the trustees absolute masters of the property and business. 

The only right accorded to the holders of certificates of stock is to share in profits or dividends. They are in the attitude of one lending money to a partnership for a share of the profits in lieu of interest. "The instrument in the instant case created a pure trust, in so far as appellants P. M. Simms and T. M. Kinser are concerned, and they are immune from individual liability." 

It is fairly evident that the court meant to hold that the shareholders in a pure trust are "shielded from all individual liability." 

If the suit had been an equitable proceeding by which the plaintiffs were attempting to take advantage of the rights of the trustees, the court would have had to decide whether, in the first instance, the trustees had any right to exoneration or indemnity against the cestuis, secondly, whether the trustees had surrendered their right to exoneration or indemnity by reason of the provisions of the paragraphs of the declaration of trust quoted above, and finally, whether the trustees had violated any of the legal provisions of the trust instrument. These problems will be subsequently discussed.18

§ 1144. Liability of the Property of a Business Trust 

If the trustees are sued at law and a judgment is obtained against them for a debt properly incurred while conducting the business of the trust, the execution must be levied on their personal property and not on the trust property.10 It is unfair to subject either the shareholders personally or the trust property to liability without giving them a chance to be heard in determining whether the obligation was rightly incurred, if the cause of action is contractual, and whether the trustees were negligent or personally to blame, if based on a tort action.20 If the creditor wishes to hold either the trust property or the shareholders personally liable he should go into a court of equity, making the shareholders parties defendant in his bill, and allege either that the trustees are insolvent or non-residents. In all other cases his remedy at law against the trustees individually is adequate.21

If the obligation was rightly incurred by the trustees, while acting properly as such, and they have paid it with their personal assets, they have the right to indemnity from the income of the trust property, and if this is insufficient, from the corpus of the trust. Their rights are even more extensive. They have the right of exoneration—that is, the right to pay all of such obligations in the first place with trust property. This right of exoneration includes not only all contract obligations rightly incurred but torts committed by them or their agents for which they are not personally to blame.22 But if in creating the obligation they violated some of the provisions of the declaration of trust, or the tort was the result of their own bad faith, negligence, or wilful wrong for which they are personally responsible, the trustees must bear the loss personally, and are not entitled to exoneration or indemnity in such cases.23 But even though

But the right of the creditors is an indirect one and is dependent upon the rights of the trustees. And, therefore, "this derivative right of the creditor against the cestui que trust (shareholders) and the trust estate, through the trustees, is available only where and to the extent that the trustees have a right to exoneration." Up to this point the courts are practically agreed. But in working out this derivative right of the creditors against the trust property the courts differ. been formulated. The English, and a majority of the American courts, have worked out the creditor's rights through the doctrine of subrogation. Under this theory, if the trustees are defaulters, or for any other reason are indebted to the trust estate, the rights of the creditors against the property of the trust are diminished to the extent of such indebtedness. In other words, the rights of a creditor are subject to the state of account between the trustees and the trust property although the entire indebtedness may have arisen out of a transaction distinct from the one out of which the creditor's cause arose.26 The position taken by these courts is admirably stated in one of the leading English cases. In In re Johnson 27 the testator directed his executor to carry on his business until a devisee became twenty-one years of age. In the course of the business debts were created by the defendant as trustee. The defendant was behind in his account with the trust estate. In the opinion it is said: "With regard to the point that has been argued, I understand the doctrine to be this, that where a trustee is authorized by a testator, or by a settlor-for it makes no difference-to carry on a business with certain funds which he gives to the trustee for that purpose, the creditor who trusts the executor has a right to say, 'I had the personal liability of the man I trusted, and I have also a right to be put in his place against the assets; that is, I have a right to the benefit of indemnity or lien which he has against the assets devoted to the purposes of the trade.' 

The first right is his general right by contract, because he trust-

The second right is a mere corollary to those numerous cases in equity in which persons are allowed to follow trust assets. The trust assets having been devoted to carrying on the trade it would not be right that the cestui que trust should get the benefit of the trade without paying the liabilities; therefore the court says to him, You shall not set up a trustee who may be a man of straw, and make him a bankrupt to avoid the responsibility of the assets for carrying on the trade; the court puts the creditor, so to speak, as I understand it, in the place of the trustee. But if the trustee has wronged the trust estate, that is, if he has taken money out of the assets more than sufficient to pay the debts, and instead of applying them to the payment of the debts has put them into his own pocket, then it appears to me there is no such equity, because the cestuis que trust are not taking the benefit. The trustee having pocketed the money, the title of the creditor, so to speak, to be put in the place of the trustee, is a title to get nothing, because nothing is due to the trustee. 

It does not appear to me that in that case the creditor, who has never contracted for anything, who has only got the benefit of this equity, if I may say so, by means of the trustee, through the lucky accident of there being a trust, ought to be put in a better position than any other creditor. I do not see that any judge has said so. "If the right of the creditors is, as is stated by Lord Justice Turner, the right to put themselves, so to speak, in the place of a trustee, who is entitled to an indemnity, of course, if the trustee is not entitled, except on terms to make good a loss to the trust estate, the creditors cannot have a better right. They do get some additional benefit so as to avoid a supposed injustice; but the injustice to be avoided is the injustice of the cestui que trust walking off with the assets which have been earned by the use of the property of the creditors; but where the cestui que trust does not get that benefit, there is no injustice as between him and the creditors, and there is no reason for the court interfering at the instance of the creditors to give them a larger 191

right than that they bargained for, namely, their personal right against the trustee. It appears to me, therefore, that if the trustee has no such right in such a case, they have none here." 

The same doctrine is followed in Massachusetts and the other jurisdictions from which cases are cited above.28 In Mason v. 

Pomeroy,29 Theodore Pomeroy devised his manufacturing property to three trustees, in trust to carry on the business until his son should become twenty-one years of age, at which time the property was to be turned over to the latter. Debts were incurred by the trustees in conducting the business and a creditor's bill was filed against them. The court held that the trustees were individually liable for all debts incurred by them while acting as such and that the creditors should be subrogated to the rights of the trustees. In the opinion it is said: "That is to say, where trustees who are authorized to carry on a business contract debts, they are not only liable personally for the payment of them, but the creditors may also resort to the trust fund, subject, however, to the rules of equity, as applicable to the facts and circumstances which may exist in any particular case. the trustees owed Grubbs and Worancy for legal services rendered the trustee. The court held that the attorneys should be paid out of the trust funds even though the trustee was a defaulter. In Owens v. Mitchell,38 Mitchell was guardian of the estate of the two Briscoes. Plaintiff was employed by Mitchell as overseer of a plantation belonging to the estate. It was agreed that plaintiff's services were worth $1,000. Plaintiff alleged that 

Mitchell was insolvent and asked a decree enforceable against the property of the minors. The district court held that the property was not liable but the Supreme Court reversed this holding. The court said: "Mitchell's insolvency is set up in the petition, and the plaintiff claims a judgment that shall bind the estate of the Briscoes, which they resist; but upon what ground of equity they should resist the payment of this debt, we are unable to discover. They are trustees of the estate lately held and managed for them by their guardian for all just creditors who have valid claims against the guardian in his fiduciary capacity (2 Story Eq. 687), and the property is ultimately liable if the guardian failed to pay it. If, then as is alleged, the guardian is insolvent, and the claim is a just one, and the estate has passed into the hands of the Briscoes themselves, their guardian being discharged from his trust, they are bound to pay it. 

37. 54 S.W. 966, 21 Ky.Law Rep. 38. 38 Tex. 589. 1258, 1259. 196

"If, on the other hand, Mitchell is still their guardian, and there are assets remaining in his hands, the judgment already against Mitchell should be paid out of such assets. "A court of equity will not allow parties, who are liable for a debt, to shirk and avoid its payment by technical objections, when all parties to be affected by the decree are properly before the court. If in such case the law, technically administered, furnishes no proper remedy, it is the peculiar province of equity to find one. "We think the court erred in sustaining the demurrer, and dismissing the Briscoes from the record."

In the article written by Mr. Justice Brandeis in which he gives the history of the Georgia holding, it is stated that the above case of Owens v. Mitchell shows that Texas follows the Georgia holding.39 It is hoped that Justice Brandeis is correct, but in 

Owens v. Mitchell the plaintiff's suit was against a guardian, and it is barely possible that the Texas Supreme Court may distinguish the cases on that ground. As Professor Williston says, "the common law at least recognized the possibility of a judgment against an executor or administrator as such, by virtue of which execution would issue against the goods of the deceased, but no similar judgment against a trustee was possible at law." 40 

The Texas Supreme Court could say that the same rules that govern in a suit against an "executor or administrator" are applicable where a "guardian" is sued.41 But no such distinction should be made, as Owens v. Mitchell was an equitable proceeding to subject "the property that was ultimately liable" for the obligation to the payment thereof, and is based on that fundamental principle of economics and law which demands that the fund or person that gets all the benefits of a business should bear its burdens. Surely, in the case of a business trust, the fund that the creditors contribute to should be primarily liable for its debts regardless of the state of accounts between the trustees and the

§ 1145. Liability of the Shareholders 

If the property of the Massachusetts trust is insufficient to pay all of the obligations of the trustees, properly incurred, have the trustees the right to exoneration against the stockholders individually? We have already seen that the creditors of the company generally have no direct legal right against either the trust property or the shareholders individually for the debts of the trustees, as the trustees are principals and not agents of the shareholders. But if the trustees have the right to exoneration against the shareholders for all debts properly incurred and tort obligations for which they are not personally to blame, the creditors may, by seeking relief, take advantage of this equitable right of the trustees and thereby the shareholders are subjected to an indirect personal liability for the debts of the company. 52 

That the shareholders are under a personal obligation to exonerate the trustees for all of such debts has been the settled law of England for many years, if the trustees did not surrender this right by a special provision to that effect in the declaration of trust.53 However the English courts have not been absolutely

Belilios,55 decided in 1901, a firm of stockholders transferred shares of stock, not fully paid, to the plaintiff. The brokers sold their equitable interest in the stock to a syndicate which transferred its interest to the defendant. 

The corporation became insolvent and plaintiff was forced to pay several calls on the stock, and brought suit for reimbursement against the defendant (cestui que trust). In holding the defendant liable the highest court of England said: "The next step is to consider on what principles an absolute beneficial owner of trust property can throw upon his trustee the burdens incidental to its ownership. The plainest principles of justice require that the cestui que trust who gets all the benefit of the property should bear its burdens unless he can show some good reason why his trustee should bear them himself. 

The obligation is equitable and not legal, and the legal decisions negativing it, unless there is some contract or custom imposing the obligation, are wholly irrelevant and beside the mark. Even where the trust property is settled on tenant for life and children, the right of their trustee to be indemnified out of the whole trust estate against any liabilities arising out of any part of it is clear and indisputable. 

Where the only cestui que 

trust is a person sui juris, the right of the trustee to indemnity by him against liabilities incurred by the trustee by his retention of the trust property has never been limited to the trust him in the administration of the trust, he is not entitled to indemnity from the beneficiary personally, unless there was an agreement either in specific words or otherwise between the trustee and the beneficiary that the beneficiary would indemnify the trustee. "(2) If the trustee is entitled to indemnity out of the trust estate for expenses incurred in the administration of the trust and conveys the trust estate to the beneficiary without deducting the amount to which he is entitled as indemnity, he is entitled to indemnity from the beneficiary personally to the extent of the property so conveyed, unless he manifested an intention to forego his claim to indemnity, or unless the beneficiary has so changed his position that it is inequitable to compel him to indemnify the trustee."
