The art to: property; it extends further and imposes upon the cestui que trust a personal obligation enforceable in equity to indemnify his trustee. This is no new principle, but is as old as trusts themselves. "In this case their Lordships have only to deal with a person sui juris beneficially entitled to shares which he cannot disclaim. 

The obligation of such a person to indemnify his trustees against calls upon them appears to their Lordships indisputable in a court of equity unless, of course, there is some contract or other circumstance which excludes such obligation. Here there is none."

It should be noted that the Privy Council held the defendant liable although he was the assignee of the parties who originally induced the plaintiff to take the stock as trustee, and that equity imposed the obligation on the cestui que trust as a result of the relation of trustee and cestui que trust in the absence of a provision in the declaration of trust to that effect. Just as a court of equity compels the principal to indemnify his agent for all expenses incident to the relation, and the husband to pay for the wife's necessaries, the court of equity, as a result of the relationship, imposes the duty of exonerating the trustees of all obligations properly incurred by them as the corollary of their right to all the profits of the business, where the trust property is insufficient. The agent is paid fully for the services that he renders the principal, and has the right of exoneration and indemnification for all obligations properly incurred.56 The trustees of a business trust are paid no more than a reasonable salary for the services actually rendered, no more than they would be paid as agents of a joint stock company for identically the same work. The trustees of a private trust, in many cases, refuse to take any salary or commission. Why, then, should a court of equity impose upon trustees the duty of insurers without paying them the customary premium? Why should not those who really own the business, and reap all its benefits, bear its burdens? There can be but one answer to these questions, 56. Mechem on Agency, § 1603 et seq. (2d Ed.). 203

§ 

Ch. 26

especially in the case of the business trust, and that, the one given by the House of Lords in the above case.57 Possibly Chief 

Justice Stone is overzealous, and goes too far in contending that the trust property should bear all the burdens incident to the administration of the trust business, including tort obligations for which the trustees are personally to blame.58 But surely the principle is sound that in a business trust the trust property and the shareholders should share the burdens of the business, at least those incurred by the trustees in the proper execution of their trust.

Section 249 of the Restatement of Trusts may represent the better view as to strictly private trusts where the cestui had no hand in the creation of the trust. Liability on the part of the cestui que trust may discourage the creation of many worthwhile private trusts. Very often it is for the best interest of the public that the owner should assign his property to a trustee for certain beneficiaries who are unable to handle the business properly. As the trustee may reject the trust if he is unwilling to pocket the losses, where he is unable so to manage the business that the debts exceed the value of the property assigned to him, if he undertakes the trust he should not be permitted to recover against the other assets that belong to the cestui que trust. In many cases the cestuis que trust are minors and cannot determine whether their estate is being properly administered by the trustee.

In the case of the business trust the situation is entirely different from that of the private trust. The shareholders create the trust and attempt to run a business without personal liability, and in many cases deliberately select trustees who own no property outside of their exemptions. In many other respects, as is shown in the preceding sections in this chapter, there is little resemblance between the private and business trust. For these reasons the courts and lawyers should not insist that the liability of the cestui que trust should be identical in both trusts.

Although the Restatement of Trusts takes the position that there is no right to indemnity against the cestuis que trust, the question has not been squarely presented to the American courts, and such statements as have been made give no real insight to the ultimate result in America.59 In business trusts the attempt has always been to hold the shareholders personally liable on a theory of partnership, consequently the question has not been raised in connection with business trusts. And in most private trusts the object of the trust is accomplished before the debts exceed the value of the property and the trustee, in a majority of cases, does not invest the funds in a hazardous business, but either lends the money on first mortgage securities or invests the funds in income bearing real estate. In Poland v. Beal 63 the shareholders of a Massachusetts trust agreed to furnish the trustees $4,000 to buy some hotel furniture that was needed by the company. The court held that the creditor, from whom the trustees purchased the furniture, could sue the trustees and those shareholders who agreed to advance the $4,000 and by taking advantage of the trustee's equitable asset, recover against such shareholders. When one is asked to become a trustee, is there not from the very nature of the relation, an implied contract on the part of the cestui que trust to exonerate the trustee for all obligations properly incurred? 

Nothing seems more just and reasonable. Courts of equity quite often read between the lines of a contract and imply conditions in law where "the inherent justice of the situation demands.” 64 

They should, in this instance, imply a contract on the part of the cestuis que trust to exonerate the trustees because it is the height of injustice to compel the trustees to pocket the losses of a business that in reality belongs to the shareholders. No honest shareholder would hesitate to exonerate the trustees for all obligations rightly incurred. What honesty demands the law should prescribe.

It is agreed by practically all authorities that there is a difference in the liability of a settlor of a trust (who is not also a cestui que trust), and the cestui que trust, to indemnify the trustee. It is settled that the trustee has no right of indemnity against the creator of a trust in the absence of an express or implied provision in the declaration of trust to that effect. But in England at least it is also settled that the trustee has a right of indemnity against the shareholders sui juris unless this right is released by the trustees. This explains the apparent conflict between the quotation set out above from Hardoon v. Belilios and that of Lord Blackburn in the case of Fraser v. Murdock,"1 where he said: "Unless there be an express or implied bargain for indemnity from the maker of the trust, he (the trustee) must be taken to accept the trust relying upon the trust funds." 

In the first case the trustee was asking indemnity from the cestui que trust, while in Fraser v. Murdock he sued the settlor of the trust for indemnity. This also is the explanation of Jones v. Walker, and many other partnership cases which hold that the executor of a deceased partner who takes an active part in the partnership business in pursuance of the agreement of the partners, is not entitled to indemnity from the general assets of the testator but only from that part of the estate invested in the firm's business for debts created after the testator's death,73 unless the will makes all the estate liable for these obligations.74

In Cox v. Hickman 75 and Wells-Stone Mercantile Co. v. Grover,76 the only question involved was the liability at law of the socalled cestuis que trust, the plaintiffs basing their entire case on the proposition that the trustees and beneficiaries were partners. The liability of the cestuis que trust to indemnify the trustees was not, in the remotest, involved in those cases. When the latter case was reversed the plaintiff amended his petition and sought to hold the secured creditors liable to the extent of the dividends that had been paid them. The court said: "The theory of this action is that these defendants have received money from the proceeds of the trust property which they cannot, in equity, withhold from this plaintiff.' The plaintiff nowhere in the petition asked for equitable relief against the defendant cestuis que trust on the ground that they should reimburse the trustee for all obligations properly incurred. The court did not discuss anything except the exact issue before it, that is, the duty of the secured creditors to return dividends improperly given them by the trustee, and the right of the creditors to be subrogated to the right of the trustee against the trust property. 

As Mr. Scott 78 and Mr. Bogert "9 have stated, if the cestuis que trust are to be liable to indemnify the trustee in any case, they should be liable in the business trust. But as stated above, in 

America the attempt has always been to hold the shareholders liable as partners, and not by way of equitable proceeding to enforce the trustees' right to indemnity. Thus the liability has always depended upon a finding of partnership. In a jurisdiction like Texas which has repudiated the business trust the question of the cestuis' liability to indemnify the trustee no longer exists, and the liability imposed upon shareholders is simply that of shareholders in a joint-stock company.

In any event a shareholder should be liable only in proportion to his interest in the trust for his pro rata share of the obligations of the company.80 

The English courts have said several times that the trustees may release or surrender their right to exoneration. In the above quotation from Hardoon v. Belilios the House of Lords said: "The obligation of such a person (cestui que trust) to indemnify his trustee appears to their Lordships indisputable in a court of equity unless, of course, there is some contract or other circumstance which excludes such obligation. Here there is none." And in Ex parte Chippendale 81 the court said: "No doubt, a company's deed, or other deed, may be so framed, as to deprive directors or trustees of the right to indemnity, and, if parties think proper to accept directorships or trusts under deeds so framed, they must abide by the consequences; but the right of indemnity is incident to the position of a trustee, and if it is sought to exclude that right, the provisions for that purpose must, as I apprehend, be clearly expressed." This question has not been settled by the American courts; in fact, the writer has found no discussion of it in any of the American cases. But Professor Stevens contends that since this right is an equitable asset in the hands of the trustees they may give it away unless this is "attempted at such time and in such manner as to impair the rights of existing creditors of the trustees." 82 In other words, he insists that "this equitable obligation to indemnify is unquestionably a liability that is subject to contractual control," and that the only restriction on the trustees' right to give this asset away, is that they cannot do so if their intent is to hinder, delay or defraud their creditors. Obviously statutes which prevent a debtor from transferring his property to hinder, delay or defraud his creditors apply in this instance.88 Professor Stevens considers the matter from the standpoint of the "obligation of the cestui que trust” rather than "the power" of the trustee, as Chief Justice Stone evidently would do. All the rules of fraudulent conveyances apply where the trustees give away this "power of indemnity." Therefore, if it is given away when the business trust is first organized and while the company is not in debt with no intent to hinder its creditors the latter could not have the conveyance set aside, but if surrendered with the intent to hinder, delay or defraud even subsequent creditors, it could be set aside.87 

In a business trust why do the shareholders insist that such a provision be inserted in the declaration of trust? Clearly, for no purpose other than to exempt themselves from personal liability for the obligations of a business in which they are vitally interested. By the surrender of trustees' right to indemnity a more burdensome duty is thereby thrown upon the trustees in conducting the trust estate and in forcing the trustees to assume this additional burden the shareholders could have but one purpose in view, and that is, to reap the benefits of the business without being personally liable for any of its obligations. American courts finally decide that the trustees can release their right to exoneration against both the trust estate and the shareholders, and that is done, and suppose further that the three trustees own no stock of the company and each is worth $100, and owes no debts at the time they are appointed trustees but the business is such that they contemplate a large indebtedness will be incurred. Theoretically it may be said that contractual creditors deal with the company with their eyes open, and, therefore, should not be permitted to set the conveyance aside. In Texas there is no statute which provides that the stock of a joint stock company must be sold at par. Such a statute is not required or necessary as each member of a joint stock company is individually liable for all the debts of the company. For the above reason the owners of property, such as an oil lease, may put a prospective value on their property and assign to themselves all of the stock of the company that they organize. Therefore, where they make a contract to give one-third of the stock to a driller and keep all the remaining stock for their oil lease, and they and the driller form the company, no one can complain since the rights of the parties depend on their contract.⁹ 

In the joint stock company, as in the corporation, it is generally provided that shares of stock can be transferred only upon the books of the company, but in the absence of any provisions regulating the sale and transfer of stock, the legal title is passed by the transfer and delivery of the certificate by the person to whom it was issued, and it is not necessary to be transferred upon the books of the company.10 Even though there are provisions that shares of stock can be transferred only on the books of the company that does not restrict the shareholder's right to transfer his stock as against subsequent creditors, unless they extended credit to the company in reliance upon his being a stockholder."1 

A transferee would not be allowed to assert the rights of a stockholder as against the company until the transfer is properly entered upon the books of the company, but a creditor may claim the advantage of that provision if (and only if) he has extended credit in reliance upon the books of the company as indicating the stockholders.

Contracts for the sale of the stock of a joint stock company, as well as subscription contracts, may be rescinded for fraud, and an allegation that the marketable value was falsely represented is sufficient grounds upon which to base an action for rescission, as such misrepresentation is one of fact and not a mere opinion. 

But where the jury finds the stock was worth the sum paid for it, and that the purchaser would have purchased the stock regardless of the representation, there is no fraud.13 

To what extent certificates of stock are negotiable, if at all, is a question of considerable uncertainty. But one thing is certain: a thief of a certificate endorsed in blank cannot transfer good title even to a bona fide purchaser for value. The endorsing in blank does not make it a bearer instrument, and one purchasing it must ascertain at his own risk that the person who is offering it for sale is either the true owner or an authorized agent of the true owner, or the purchaser must make out a case of estoppel before he is protected.14 But once the certificate has been transferred upon the books of the joint stock company and a new certificate issued, the purchasers of such reissued certificate will be protected even as against the owner of the original certificate, according to the opinion of one Court of Civil Appeals.15 The same court held that the company is not liable for the value of the stock to the original owner. The only duty upon the company is to ascertain that the endorsement is the genuine signature of the book owner. There is no duty to ascertain how the

§ 1147. Membership-Mutual Dealings and Liabilities of the 

Members

As has been stated above, one purchasing shares in a joint. stock company becomes a member (stockholder) upon the payment of the consideration even though the certificate has not been issued.¹ And from the instant of becoming a member a stockholder is charged with notice of the provisions of the articles of agreement and any by-laws that the company may have adopted.18 It may be provided in the articles of agreement that the stockholders shall be exempt from personal liability, and while this provision may not be valid as against a third party, it is binding as between themselves, and one becoming a member of the association is charged with knowledge of such provision. and will not be allowed to hold the individual members liable upon a claim arising simultaneous with, or subsequent to his becoming a member.19 But he is not precluded from recovery upon a claim which arose previous to his becoming a member.20

Ch. § 1148 

Although stockholders in an unincorporated association or joint stock company are in many respects treated as partners, they may vest the legal title of its property and the active management in one of their number or in a board of directors or trustees,21 and this is the ordinary manner of conducting the business of such companies. Such managing officers or trustees are liable to removal for misconduct in office, and may be enjoined for wasteful misconduct by suit of the individual stockholders.22

Withdrawal of stockholders does not effect a dissolution of a joint stock company,23 and an accounting is not necessary upon the retirement of a stockholder. What property is to be treated as firm capital or as individual property for purposes of retirement or dissolution may be determined by contract.24 

In determining who are members it has been held that the holder of "full-paid preferred stock" is a member and not a creditor, and a provision that the holders of preferred stock are not entitled to vote is valid and immaterial on the issue of whether the plaintiff is a shareholder or a creditor.25

Ch. § 1150 

The trustees or directors are in most cases given the power to act for and bind the company, and the acts of the trustees bind the company 51 even though they have vested the active management of the company in a general manager or other officers. 

When certain authority is vested in a general manager or other officers, they can bind the company only within the limits of that authority, and the company may set up lack of authority as a defense to suits arising out of their acts beyond their authority.52 But if the company retains the benefits of unauthorized acts of its officers, it will be liable therefor on the ground of ratification.53 A person serving the company in a dual capacity may bind the company by acts which are authorized as to one office but not as to the other.54 Unauthorized acts may be ratified by the board of directors or trustees, and a formal meeting is not necessary; acquiescence is sufficient.55 Shareholders as such have no power to act for and bind the company.56

"Where suit shall be brought against such company or association, and the only service had shall be upon the president, secretary, treasurer or general agent of such company or association, and judgment shall be rendered against the defendant company, such judgment shall be binding on the joint property of all the stockholders or members thereof, and may be enforced by execution against the joint property; but such judgment shall not be binding on the individual property of the stockholders or members, nor authorize execution against it."

Golden West Oil Co. No. 1 v. Golden 

Rod Oil Co. No. 1, Tex.Civ.App., 285 S.W. 631, judgment affirmed, 285 S.W. 627, and order affirmed,

Golden West Oil Co. No. 1, Com.

Phoenix Oil Co. v. Illinois Torpedo 

Co., Tex.Civ.App., 261 S.W. 487. 

Article 6137. "In a suit against such company or association, in addition to service on the president, secretary, treasurer or general agent of such companies or association, service of citation may also be had on any and all of the stockholders or members of such companies or associations; and, in the event judgment shall be against such unincorporated company or association, it shall be equally binding upon the individual property of the stockholders or members so served, and executions may issue against the property of the individual stockholders or members, as well as against the joint property; but executions shall not issue against the individual property of the stockholders or members until execution against the joint property has been returned without satisfaction."

Article 6138. "The provisions of this chapter shall not affect nor impair the right allowed unincorporated joint stock companies and associations to sue in the individual names of the stockholders or members, nor the right of any person to sue the individual stockholders or members; but the provisions of this chapter shall be construed as cumulative merely of other remedies now existing under the law."

§ 1161. In General 

There are several Federal statutes that must be examined by the lawyer, especially when he contemplates the promotion or reorganization of a corporation. The most important ones will be discussed briefly in this chapter. At this time most reorganizations of private corporations are brought about under Chapter 

10 of the Chandler Act, 11 U.S.C.A. § 501 et seq. In order to understand that act a brief summary of 77B, 11 U.S.C.A. § 207, is very helpful. 229

§ Ch. 27 

FEDERAL LEGISLATION § 1162. Section 77B of National Bankruptcy Act-Purpose 

On June 7, 1934, the President approved the Act of Congress ¹ which was passed to facilitate corporate reorganizations. The main underlying reason and purpose of the amendment was "to afford aid in the effort to rehabilitate corporations solvent in fact but unable to meet maturing obligations." "It was not the purpose to lend its aid generally and without discrimination to corporations hopelessly insolvent, and without legal resources to prosecute their business with reasonable prospect of success." 3 "Section 77B gives the debtor the right to file an original petition. This is the first and primary purpose in the act. 

The debtor may also file an answer to a creditor's petition." 4 "Before the adoption of Section 77B, the sole means of reorganization was in equity with its cumbersome incidents and uncertain outcome. The reform effected by the bankruptcy amendment was to provide that a plan approved by the court and acceptable to a certain majority should be compulsory. Its effect has been to supersede equity receiverships incident to reorganization." 5 Another reason for the passage of section 77B was that

"The purpose of the Act is to protect the interests of the debtor in case he is not insolvent but merely unable to meet his debts as they mature; to keep the property or business intact if that may be done; to provide for the reorganization of the debtor corporation and the development of a plan by the terms of which the debtor, its stockholders, and the creditors may receive fair and reasonable treatment."

Constitutionality

The federal courts have upheld in general the constitutionality of section 77B, and the act is given a liberal construction in determining the meaning of its provisions.10 Section 77B is not unconstitutional even though it empowers the bankruptcy court to require minority nonconsenting creditors of a particular class to accept any major modification of their original contractual relation.11 Nor is section 77B an unconstitutional encroachment 

10. Campbell v. Alleghany Corporation, C.C.A.Md., 75 F.2d 947, 952, 953: "The grant of power to Congress to establish uniform laws on the subject of bankruptcies is not limited to the forms in which that power has heretofore been exercised by Congress or by the laws relating to bankruptcy which had been enacted in England or in the several American Colonies prior to the adoption of the constitution. * * All phases of the relationship between a debtor financially embarrassed and his creditors are brought under the control of Congress by the constitutional grant of power; and the fact that a particular mode has hitherto been employed in dealing with this relationship is not to be taken as a measure of the power over it." "As pointed out by the Supreme

ization, such as is provided for by the statute here, involves nothing more than is done in an ordinary bankruptcy proceeding when a composition agreement is made binding upon the nonassenting minority of creditors; and there can be no question as to the constitutionality of such composition provisions of the bankruptcy statute." 

The same court on page 950 of 75 

F.2d said: "The statute is of a remedial character, designed to facilitate the reorganization of corporate business made necessary by the economic depression through which the country has been passing. Its purpose should be forwarded by a fair and liberal construction of its provisions, not thwarted by any narrow or technical interpretation, and certainly not by reading into its language conditions and limitations which the lawmakers themselves did not see fit to express. "And we entertain no doubt as to the constitutionality of the statute.

It is an exercise of the power conferred on Congress by Article I, section 8, cl. 4 of the Constitution, 'to establish * * uniform laws on the subject of Bankruptcies throughout the United States,' adopted to the conditions presented by modern industrial organization." In the light of these excerpts from the opinion of the court it is interesting to know that the United States

FEDERAL LEGISLATION § 1165. 

State Court Proceedings and Section 77B 

When bankruptcy proceedings have been instituted, the federal court acquires jurisdiction of all of the debtor's property throughout the United States to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of all other courts. Consequently, a creditor cannot proceed in a state court to enforce his judgment lien which he acquired after the petition in bankruptcy was filed.19 "The jurisdiction of a 

Federal Court of Bankruptcy is exclusive, and it supersedes the jurisdiction of the state court with respect to all the debtor's property. 

That jurisdiction cannot be defeated by the fact that the state court has assumed jurisdiction of a suit for fraud against the debtor in which he is about to render, or even has rendered, a judgment which is not subject to discharge in bankruptcy."20 However, the bankruptcy court does not acquire jurisdiction over the properties of a solvent subsidiary of the debtor corporation and therefore the court cannot enjoin a suit against the subsidiary corporation which is not involved in

One court very succintly construed the rights of a lessor under section 77B in the following manner: "Under section 77B (b) (10), 11 U.S.C.A. § 207 (b) (10), landlord's claims for injury from the refection of an unexpired lease of real estate or for damages or indemnity under a covenant in the lease are to be treated like debts provable under section 63a, 11 U.S. 

C.A. § 103 (a); the amount allowable not to exceed the rent, without acceleration, reserved for the three years next succeeding the date of surrender to the landlord, unless he has previously re-entered when that date is taken as the base instead, plus unpaid rent then accrued. While it is plain that claims for future rent are provable in 77B reorganization proceedings where they would not have been under the act as it stood previously, it is equally plain that whatever change in this respect was made had to do only with the remedy. It is necessary to have a claim against a debtor which the substantive law of landlord and tenant recognizes as an enforceable claim in order to have a provable claim under section 77B. That section does not extend the liability of a lessee beyond what it otherwise would be under applicable law. If under such law a landlord would have a claim against a lessee for damages or indemnity under a covenant contained in a lease which would have been recoverable in a civil action had there been no 77B petition approved, such claim may be proved in the 77B proceedings and allowed to the limited extent above indicated. Likewise where an executory contract or an unexpired lease has been rejected pursuant to the direction of the judge in such a proceeding or by a trustee or receiver in bankruptcy or a receiver in equity in a proceeding pending before the 77B petition was filed. But there is no new definition of a claim; only of a creditor. A landlord having a claim under the applicable state law of the nature set forth in section 77B (b) (10) is a creditor under section 77B

with a creditor's rights thereunder, including, of course, the right to prove and have his claim allowed. "It follows that, as none of the claims arose from the rejection of leases and all the original leases upon which they are based were terminated by agreement of the parties before these proceedings were instituted, and, indeed, before Section 77B was passed, and the leased real estate surrendered to and accepted by the landlords without any reservation of rights under the leases against the lessee, this debtor, the lessors, have no valid claims for future rent. "The issue here is not one of the provability of actual claims for future rent, but rather one of recognition that the claimants have no claims at all against the debtor or its estate. Before

The power to grant stays in aid of a reorganization is thus far more sweeping than the power granted in ordinary cases of bankruptcy. * * * "But the claim of Foust as administrator is dischargeable in a 77B proceeding so that there was power to enjoin its prosecution not only under 

(c) (10) of 77B (11 U.S.C.A. § 207 (c) 

(10) but under section 11 of the original Bankruptcy Act (11 U.S.C.A. 

§ 29). Section 77B (b) (10) defines creditors as 'all holders of claims of whatever character against the debtor or its property,' and clause (h), 11

U.S.C.A. § 207 (h), provides that the final decree confirming the plan of reorganization 'shall discharge the debtor from its debts and liabilities.'

It is apparent from this broad language of clauses (b) (10) and (h), supra, that a discharge of the debtor under a plan of reorganization is not dependent on whether the claim in question would be dischargeable in a strict bankruptcy proceeding but embraces liabilities of every kind whether fixed or contingent. Indeed, reorganizations would often be impracticable if the plans did not provide for a discharge of all liabilities and if resumption of business left the debtor with tort liabilities which had not been adjudicated prior to the filing of the 77B petition. The words of clause (h) granting a discharge, not only from debts, but from 'liabilities', and also the language of clause (c) (6), 11 U.S.C.A. § 207 (c) (6), which requires the judge to set a time within which the claims of stockholders as well as those of creditors shall be proved, make it plain that liabilities of every kind are to be discharged in a reorganization under section 77B.

(k), dealing with an order for liquidation of the estate, where a plan of reorganization has failed, and subdivision (0), 11 U.S.C.A. § 207 (0), making the provisions of the old Bankruptcy act generally applicable in 

77B proceedings, are to be read with the limitations in clauses (b) (10), (c) (6) and (h), supra." and

A very unique situation arose in Chicago which involved the state dissolution statute and section 77B of the federal bankruptcy statute. The debtor corporation had been dissolved for longer than two years and the corporate assets, land and building, has been sold at a foreclosure sale. After the period of two years, in which the property could have been redeemed, had expired, and subsequent to the expiration of the two-year statutory period within which the dissolved corporation could have sued or have been sued, it filed a petition for reorganization under section 77B. The Federal District Court and the Circuit Court of Appeals held that since the dissolved corporation remained in existence and had not been completely liquidated, it could reorganize under section 77B. The majority opinion of the United 

States Supreme Court reversed the lower court decisions with the following language: "The court below relied upon its former decision in the case of In re 211 East Delaware Place Bldg. Corporation (C.C.A.Ill.) 

76 F.2d 834. That was a case, however, where the bankruptcy petition had been filed by creditors, not by the dissolved corporation; and, therefore, the capacity of the defunct corporation to institute proceedings was not involved. We express no opinion as to the correctness of this decision; but Judge Evans, who wrote the opinion, apparently regarded the distinction as important. For in a later proceeding in the case (D.C.Ill.) 14 F. 

Supp. 96, 100, he said that the forfeiture of the charter of the corporation did not prevent such a proceeding by creditors, and then added, "The only effect which this loss of corporate existence may have upon a bankruptcy proceeding is in respect to the inability of the corporation to admit acts of bankruptcy or state of insolvency or to file a voluntary petition.' (Italics supplied.) "The power to take the long step of putting an end to the corporate existence of a state-created corporation without limitation, connotes the power to take the shorter one of putting an end to it with such limitations as the Legislature sees fit to 

V. Van Shaick, 56 S.Ct. 142, 296 

U.S. 594, 80 L.Ed. 421.

In re New York Title & Mortgage 

Co., D.C.N.Y., 9 F.Supp. 319. 245

§

And, since the federal government is powerless to resurrect a corporation which the state has put out of existence for all purposes, the conclusion seems inevitable that, if the state attach qualifications to its sentence of extinction, nothing can be added to or taken from these qualifications by federal authority." 47

This decision seems to have been the result of a strict interpretation of the Illinois statute providing that the dissolved corporation can sue or be sued only within two years from the date of dissolution. It is not possible to make any predictions of the result of the federal court's decision should the same situation arise in Texas, because there are at least five statutory provisions providing for the continued existence of the corporation for various purposes after it has been dissolved; the length of time for which the dissolved corporation shall remain in existence for the named purposes varies from three years to a reasonable time.48

The Petition 

The petitioner is required to allege certain jurisdictional facts before the court can act irrespective of the necessity of reorganization under section 77B.55 At times the court is forced to look at all the surrounding circumstances to determine whether the petition shows good grounds for reorganization, aside from allegations of jurisdictional facts.56 Under section 77B a court of bankruptcy looks through the form to the substance of the transaction to determine whether the petition states sufficient facts to merit relief under the statute.57 The factor of insolvency or that the debtor is unable to meet the debts as they mature is another fact necessary to be alleged to avoid a dismissal of the petition.58

If the debtor has not committed an act of bankruptcy, the creditors of the debtor must state, among other averments in their petition, that a proceeding in bankruptcy or equity receivership is pending.59 The possession of a mortgagee is not the possession of an equity receiver which satisfies the requirements of the statute.60 Neither is a receivership in a foreclosure suit an equity receivership within the meaning of section 77B (a).61 

55. In re Central Public Utility 

Corp., D.C.Del., 9 F.Supp. 17: "A necessary jurisdictional averment prescribed by the statute is that the debtor has committed an act of bankruptcy within four months, unless a prior proceeding in bankruptcy or equity receivership is pending and is averred as pending. There is no averment that such proceeding is pending. It follows that the petition is fatally defective in failing to aver that the debtor has committed an act of bankruptcy within four months."

In Consolidated Rock Products Co. v. Du Bois, 312 U.S. 510, 61 S.Ct. 675, 85 L.Ed. 982, Justice Douglas said: 

"The Circuit Court of Appeals held that the absolute priority rule of 

Northern Pacific Ry. Co. v. Boyd, 228 

U.S. 482, 33 S.Ct. 554, 57 L.Ed. 931, and Case of Los Angeles Lumber 

Products Co., 308 U.S. 106, 60 S.Ct. 1, 84 L.Ed. 110, applied to reorganizations of solvent as well as insolvent companies. That is true. Whether a company is solvent or insolvent in either the equity or the bankruptcy sense, 'any arrangement of the parties by which the subordinate rights and interests of the stockholders are attempted to be secured at the expense of the prior rights' of creditors *comes within judicial denunciation.' 

Louisville Trust Co. v. Louisville, N. 

A. & C. Ry. Co., 174 U.S. 674, 684, 19 

S.Ct. 827, 43 L.Ed. 1130. And we indicated in Case v. Los Angeles Lumber Products Co., supra, that that rule was not satisfied even though the relative priorities' of creditors and stockholders were maintained. "The instant plan runs afoul of that principle. In the first place, no provision is made for the accrued interest on the bonds. This interest is entitled to the same priority as the principal. See American Iron &

Steel Mfg. Co. v. Seaboard Air Line 

Ry., 233 U.S. 261, 266-267, 34 S.Ct. 

502, 58 L.Ed. 949; Ticonic National 

Bank v. Sprague, 303 U.S. 406, 58 S. 

Ct. 612, 82 L.Ed. 926. In the second place, and apart from the cancellation of interest, the plan does not satisfy the fixed principle of the 

Boyd case even on the assumption that the enterprise as a whole is solvent in the bankruptcy sense. The bondholders for the principal amount of their 6% bonds receive an equal face amount of new 5% income bonds and preferred stock, while the preferred stockholders receive new common stock. True, the relative priorities are maintained. But the bondholders have not been made whole. 

They have received an inferior grade of securities, inferior in the sense that the interest rate has been reduced, a contingent return has been substituted for a fixed one, the maturities have been in part extended and in part eliminated by the substitution of preferred stock, and their former strategic position has been weakened. 

Those lost rights are of value. Full compensatory provision must be made for the entire bundle of rights which the creditors surrender. "The absolute priority rule does not mean that bondholders cannot be given inferior grades of securities, or 251

§ 

Ch. 27

FEDERAL LEGISLATION 

tion which is indefinite and uncertain.73 

The findings of the bankruptcy court with regard to the proposed plan for reorganization and the court's confirmation of the plan will not be disturbed, especially if the interested parties had notice of all the proceedings but failed to object to the even securities of the same grade as are received by junior interests. Requirements of feasibility of reorganization plans frequently necessitate it in the interests of simpler and more conservative capital structures. And standards of fairness permit it. This was recognized in Kansas City Terminal Ry. Co. v. Central Union Trust 

Co., 271 U.S. 445, 46 S.Ct. 549, 70 I

Ed. 1028. This Court there said (p. 

455) that though 'to the extent of their debts creditors are entitled to priority over stockholders against all the property' of the debtor company, 'it does not follow that in every re organization the securities offered to general creditors must be superior in rank or grade to any which stockholders may obtain. It is not impossible to accord to the creditor his superior rights in other ways.' And the 

Court went on to say (p. 456), 'No offer is fair which does not recognize the prior rights of creditors ; but circumstances may justify an offer of different amounts of the same grade of securities to both creditors and stockholders."

Thus it is plain that while creditors may be given inferior grades of securities, their 'superior rights' must be recognized. Clearly, those prior rights are not recognized, in cases where stockholders are participating in the plan, if creditors are given only a face amount of inferior securities equal to the face amount of their claims. They must receive, in addition, compensation for the senior rights which they are to surrender. If they receive less than that full compensatory treatment, some of their property rights will be appropriated for the benefit of stockholders without compensation. That is not permissible. The plan then comes within judicial denunciation because it does not recognize the creditors' 'equitable right to be preferred to stockholders against the full value of all property belonging to the debtor corporation.' Kansas City Terminal 

Ry. Co. v. Central Union Trust Co., 271 U.S. 445, 46 S.Ct. 549, 70 L.Ed. 1028."

Property Rights and Assets 

The chattels held by the debtor under a conditional sales contract at the time of the filing of the petition under section 77B is not "property" and cannot be the subject-matter of reorganization proceedings.99 "Property” as defined in the reorganization section of the Bankruptcy Act has been construed to include only the property of the debtor; consequently property held in trust by the bankrupt cannot be included in the administration of the settlor's estate under section 77B.¹ But a taxpayer's right of redemption of property from a tax sale is a "property right" and is an "asset" within the meaning of the Bankruptcy Act dealing with reorganization of corporations. A trustee under a deed of trust, after default, takes possession as owner and not as a receiver, and he cannot be ousted under proceedings under section 77B; therefore, it is error for a court to order the mortgaged property turned over to the temporary trustee in attempting to effect a reorganization.³

Jurisdiction of the Court 

When a Federal District Court acquires jurisdiction in reorganization proceedings under section 77B, it has jurisdiction of all the corporation's property throughout the United States in preference to any state or federal receiver previously appointed in any other proceeding, and the court has the power to order that the property be turned over to the trustee appointed by that court. In order to effect this result the court has been given the power to issue its process throughout the United States; however, the court does not have the power to issue process throughout the United States when the debtor corporation has only a cause of action in personam against the defendant.5 The court, after acquiring jurisdiction of the debtor corporation, has the power to authorize the purchase of goods; the expenditures for such purchases will be treated as administration expenses, and provide that such expenses may be made prior to the rights of mortgage lien holders. The District Court is bound by the decision of the referee in a matter which was not within his jurisdiction." But if the highest state court renders a decision which fixed the rights and obligations of the parties with respect to a guaranteed mortgage involving trust property lying in that state, the District Court is bound by that decision. Ch. § 1178 

FEDERAL LEGISLATION § 1178. The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 

Securities Act of 1933 21 was intended for the protection of the buyer of newly issued securities by requiring a full disclosure of material facts as of the time the security was issued. 

The act applied only where the financing is to be done by a public offering of securities as distinguished from the private placement of securities with a small group of individual investors or investment institutions. It is to be noticed that the act contained no provision requiring issuers of securities registered under it to supply investors with current information about the securities. A rider to the Securities Exchange Act of 1934,22 which established Federal regulation of stock exchanges, supplemented the protection given the investor by requiring that the facts be kept up to date by supplemental statements at annual or more frequent intervals. 

Under the Securities Exchange Act, corporations which desire to have their securities listed on an exchange must file a public document containing the registration statement with the exchange and with the Commission, and must also make such annual and other periodic reports of their financial condition as the Commission may require.23 One of the most significant powers of the Commission is that of prescribing the form of reports and the item details of the financial statements.24 The Commission may also stipulate the methods for determining depreciation, recurring and non-recurring income, and the like.25

Before a securities exchange is allowed to transact business it must be registered with the Commission. "The Commission may deny, suspend, or revoke any registration, and it likewise has power to compel registered exchanges to make such changes of their rules and practices as the Commission may deem necessary to insure fair dealings on such exchange." 26 For violation by any exchange of a provision of the act, or a failure to enforce insofar as it can compliance with the rules of the Commission, the Commission may suspend for a period not exceeding twelve months, or withdraw completely the registration of the exchange. Such penalties may also be imposed upon a member of an exchange or an insurer who fails to comply with any provision of the act.

To control the flow of credit to the stock market, the act established control over broker's borrowing and also of the amount that brokers may lend to customers. Brokers and dealers are allowed to borrow only from banks of the Federal Reserve System; from such "out-side" banks as are willing to conform to 

Federal Reserve Act, the Banking Act of 1933, and the provisions of this act in regard to such borrowing; and from other brokers and dealers in accordance with the Federal Reserve Board. Other borrowing by a broker is severely restricted. In an emergency he is allowed to borrow from other sources but subject to the Board's regulations. However, on an exempted security a broker may borrow from any source. The broker's aggregate indebtedness incurred in the ordinary course of business may not exceed twenty times the net capital in the business.

The hypothecation of a customer's securities may be regulated by the Commission. Before a broker is allowed to commingle customer's securities for borrowing, he must secure the customer's written consent. An important change from the old law is that in no case may securities of a customer be commingled with those of the broker himself or with those of someone not a customer. The lien of the pledgee in any case must not 

26. 47 Yale L.J. 622, 625. 268

Ch. § 1178 

FEDERAL LEGISLATION 

be greater than the aggregate indebtedness of the customer in respect to the pledged security. The act forbids the broker to lend the customer's securities without the latter's consent. This provision as well as most of the hypothecation provisions is a mere re-enactment of existing law. 

One of the most controversial features of the act involved marginal requirements, i. e., the amount brokers could lend customers. The whole matter has been left in the hands of the Federal Reserve Board for rules and regulations. However, the act does establish a norm that prescribes the maximum credit that may be initially extended by a broker or dealer to a customer. These requirements suggested allow initial loans in the alternative, whichever is higher: 55% of the current market price of the security or 100% of the lowest price of the security during the preceding 35 months, but not more than 75% of the current market price.27 The Board, in addition to prescribing the marginal rules, "may also regulate the maintenance of a marginal account in general, including matters involving additional purchases, substitutions, withdrawals, arbitrage, transfers, undermarginal accounts, short sales, and the like." 28

Section 10 forbids short sales of a security registered on a national exchange except as such transactions are allowed under the regulations of the Commission. Short sales are forbidden to officers, directors, and stockholders owning as much as ten per cent of the corporate stock.29 As short selling has been recognized as one of the most important evils of stock exchange practices, it was expected that the Commission would respect the Congressional opinion and limit short sales to exceptional cases. 

One of the most interesting sections of the act is Section 14, which seems to have as its object to make more effective the voting power of the individual shareholder. This section makes it unlawful for any person, by the use of the mails or any instrumentality of interstate commerce, to solicit any proxy in 

27. Meyer, The Securities Exchange

respect to any security registered on a national exchange in contravention of such rules and regulations as the Commission may prescribe. Section 14 (b) makes it unlawful for any member of an exchange or any broker or dealer who transacts business through such member to give a proxy in respect to any security carried for the account of a customer. Acting under authority of these provisions the Commission has promulgated rules that require: (1) proxies solicited on behalf of the management shall state that they are so solicited; (2) proxies that relate to the election of officers or directors shall be accompanied by a substantial amount of information about the candidate; (3) proxies that relate to changes in the rights of any class of security holders shall be accompanied by a description of the material differences which the proposed change would make, and also a statement of the current financial condition of the corporation.30

Under sections 9-11 of the act, three types of transactions have been prohibited: (1) Any series of transactions for the purpose of creating a false or misleading appearance of active trading or a false or misleading appearance with respect to the market for any security. As it is difficult to ascertain whether a sale is for a direct profit and when the purpose is to bring others into the market, it seems clear that this section will not apply unless there is a deliberate attempt at stock manipulation. (2) 

The dissimulation of information in the course of ordinary business by a broker or dealer or other person selling or offering for sale or purchasing or offering to purchase that the price of the security is likely to rise or fall by reason of individual or pool activities. (3) False or misleading statements regarding any security listed on a national exchange in order to induce the purchase or sale of such security.

These provisions apply not only to members of an exchange but also to any other person if such transactions occur in a registered exchange or use is made of the instrumentalities of interstate commerce.31 * * * The act seeks to prevent the unfair use of confidential information in two ways. Every director, officer, or the holder of more than 10% of any class of registered equity security shall file with the exchange and with the Commission a report of his shareholdings. There is provision for keeping this information current by requiring a report within ten days of the end of each calendar month if there has been a change in ownership during such period. In order to prevent unfair use of information which may have been obtained by such officer, director, or beneficial owner by reason of his relationship to the issuing corporation, the issuer is entitled to any profit made by such owner, director, or officer provided such person has sold the stock within six months of the time he bought it or if he buys it back within six months of the time he sold it. The second method for preventing insiders from using such information to the detriment of the Company is by prohibiting such officers, directors, or shareholder from selling securities of their own corporation which they do not then own, i. e., short sales, or to sell it on credit. § 1179.

FEDERAL LEGISLATION § 1180. The Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 37 

The purpose of the Public Utility Holding Company Act is to protect not only the investors in such companies and their subsidiaries but also consumers and the public in general from certain abusive practices that have arisen in financing and managing holding companies. Title 1 of the act exempts from its provisions those holding companies which, because of the nature of their organization or operation, cannot be of great importance to interstate commerce or to the national public interest. The act applies to interstate electric and gas utility holding companies and their subsidiaries. Holding companies are brought within the scope of the act, § 4, 15 U.S.C.A. § 79d, which makes interstate activities unlawful for all holding companies unless they are registered in accordance with the provisions of § 5, 15 U.S. 

C.A. § 79e.38 This registration brings the holding companies within the compass of the remainder of the act. 

The first object of the act is to change the highly pyramided companies with widely scattered utility properties into single integrated systems with less complicated capital structures. This section, in addition to being designed to eliminate unnecessary complexity in the corporate structures of holding company systems, seeks to distribute the voting power among the security holders fairly and equitably. This section provided that after January 1, 1938, the Commission was to limit holding companies to single integrated systems unless (1) such integrated systems are less economical than diversified ownership; (2) additional systems are regionalized within one power shed; and (3) the combined systems are not too large as to impair the advantages of "localized management, efficient operation, or the effectiveness of the regulation".40 

Under section 11 (b) (2) the duty is placed on the Securities and Exchange Commission to require holding companies and their subsidiaries to "take such steps as the Commission shall find necessary to ensure that the corporate structure or continued existence of any company in the holding company system does not unduly or unnecessarily complicate the structure, or unfairly or inequitably distribute the voting power among security holders of such holding company system." The so-called "great-grandfather" clause provides a definite criteria for simplification by prohibiting more than two holding companies above an operating subsidiary. It is apparent that this paragraph would serve to eliminate intermediate holding companies and top or "super" holding companies.

Section 12 institutes a thorough control over inter-company transactions between companies in the same holding company system. "Upstream" loans are absolutely forbidden, and loans by a holding company to its subsidiaries are subject to Commission control. The payment of dividends by both the holding company and its subsidiaries are possible only when they conform such rules and regulations as the Commission

§ 1181. The Investment Company Act of 1940 45 

Under penalty of exclusion from the mails and all channels of interstate commerce, investment companies are required to register with the Securities Exchange Commission. After such registration the company is subject to all of the provisions of the Investment Company Act. The definition of an investment company was arrived at by including in general terms any "issues engaged primarily in the business of investing, re-investing, or trading in securities." Provision is also made to exclude, upon application to the Commission, those companies whose holdings are in majority owned subsidiaries conducting similar types of business. However, the subsidiary must not be an investment company. [Section 3 (b) (2) (3) of the act.] Other companies are excluded either because they are classified as concerns which do not call for the type of supervision provided for in the act, or because they are already subject to regulation. 

In general, information required upon registration is similar to that required under the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934. Section 8 requires each company to make certain "recitations of policy" in the registration statement, and it is forced to adhere to this policy, unless, pursuant to section 13, a change is authorized by the shareholders. A statement of policy is also required as to any other matter which the registering company elects to treat as a matter of fundamental policy. Registration statements are required to be kept up to date with periodical reports to the Commission and to the shareholders covering such matters as remuneration of company officials, financial status of the company, the securities owned, and the like. The Commission is given the power to prescribe a “reasonable degree of uniformity" in accounting practices, both for the purpose of these periodic reports and the maintenance of complete financial records required by section 31. 

Investment Companies are classified as (1) face amount certificate companies, (2) unit investment trusts and, (3) management companies. Management companies are in turn sub-divided into open-end and closed-end companies and also diversified and non-diversified companies. 

Section 9 makes ineligible as an underwriter, broker, or majority director any person who within ten years has been convicted of a felony or misdemeanor arising out of a security transaction or any person who is either temporarily or permanently enjoined from engaging in such transactions. By section 17 it is made unlawful for any officer, promoter, principal shareholder, or director of an investment company, or any person or corporation affiliated with them to sell any security to the investment 277

§ 

Ch. 27

FEDERAL LEGISLATION 

company unless the Commission, for cause shown, exempts the particular transaction from the rule. This section further regulates participation by investment companies in underwritings of affiliated persons, and limits the compensation which any affiliated person may receive while acting as a broker for the investment company. Section 17 also makes unlawful any charter, by-law, or other provisions which purports to protect any director or officer of an investment company against liability for willful misfeasance, gross negligence, bad faith, or reckless disregard of his duty.

The purpose of section 10 is to provide for an independent board of directors and independent investment advice. This section provides that investment companies must have a minority of 40% on the board of directors who are not affiliated with the management, and must also have a majority of the directors independent of (1) brokers as a group, (2) investment bankers as a group, and (3) principal underwriters of its securities as a group. The section further provides that no investment company is permitted to have a majority of its board of directors consisting of persons who are officers or directors of any one bank. Under section 15 investment advisory and distribution contracts are limited to two years, but they may be renewed annually by action of the board of directors. Before an investment advisory contract is valid, it must be approved by a majority of the shareholders. Additional protection is given to the stockholders by section 16 (a) providing that no person may serve as a director unless elected by the shareholders, except that vacancies, not exceeding one-third of the directors, which occur between meetings may be filled in any authorized manner. The subject matter of this provision is only one of the various fundamental matters, such as management contracts and matters affecting vital changes in the policy or purpose of the company, that are required to be submitted to the vote of the stock holders. 

Section 12 prohibits a registered company from (1) effecting a short sale, (2) selling on the margin, and (3) purchasing on a joint or a joint and several basis any security. This section also prohibits an open-end company from distributing its own shares 278

Ch. § 1182 

FEDERAL LEGISLATION 

in contravention to the rules of the SEC and attempts to forbid pyramiding by investment companies. Under section 23 (c) a closed-end company may purchase its own shares on the open market after a six months' notice to its shareholders, or pursuant to tender by an entire class of stockholders, or under such other circumstances as the Commission may allow. 

Senior securities are not prohibited by the act as many had advocated, but their use has been regulated as to kind and to amount. Section 23 provides that no registered closed-end company may issue any of its securities for services or property other than for cash or securities; and the sale of common stock of which the company is the issuer at a price below market is prohibited except in certain instances enumerated in the act. The prohibition against issuing securities for other than cash or other securities would serve to abolish the common practice of exchanging choice securities for promotional expenses.

Proxy solicitations are subject to regulation by the commission. Section 18 (i) forbids the issuance of non-voting shares, and preferred shareholders must be given the right to elect at least two directors at all times, and a majority of the directors under certain instances. The act provides that dividends are to be paid only from net income, and if not so made, they shall be accompanied by a statement that discloses the source of payment. Other provisions of the act prohibit investment companies from issuing voting trust certificates; from having cross or circular ownership; or issuing warrants good for longer periods than one hundred twenty days.46

The Commission is given the power to make investigation and to hold public hearings. In case of refusal to obey a subpoena issued to any person, the Commission is authorized to invoke the aid of any court of the United States within the jurisdiction. If it appears to the Commission that a person has or is about to violate any provisions of the act it may enjoin such acts or practices. The Commission is also authorized to transmit evidence of such violations to the Attorney-General, who may, in his discretion, institute appropriate criminal proceedings. The act provides that any person who willfully violates any of its provisions shall be subject to a fine of not more than $10,000, or imprisonment for two years, or both. The Commission is given authority to "make, issue, amend, or rescind, such rules and regulations and such orders as are necessary and appropriate to the exercise of the powers conferred upon the Commission. 

Such orders "shall issue only after appropriate notice and an opportunity for a hearing." Any person aggrieved by an order of the Commission may secure a judicial review of such order by filing in either the appropriate circuit court of appeals or the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia "a written petition praying that the order of the Commission be modified or set aside in whole or in part". 281

§ 1183.

Federal Income Tax as Affecting Corporate Reorganizations In reorganizing a corporation special attention should be given to the reorganization sections of the Federal Income Tax Law. 

In a general work on Corporations it is impossible to "scratch the surface" of this subject, but attention should be directed to several provisions of the Internal Revenue Code. 

The general rule of the Capital Gains Law is to tax the difference between the cost of an asset and the value of what is received for it. After the 1916 Tax Act it was found that reorganizations could constitute exchanges under the general meaning of the term exchanges in the act. It was to avoid taxation of such exchanges "that Congress, beginning with the 1918 Act, made special provision exempting reorganizations from the general rule making exchanges taxable." 48 In order that the gains realized in a reorganization may be tax free, the reorganization must comply with the standards enumerated in Section 112 of the Revenue Act of 1938.49

This section treats the subject of gains or loss resulting from the sale or exchange of property. The entire amount of such gain or loss, determined under section 111, is recognized as subject to the capital gains tax, except as provided in this section. 

Under section (b) (3) "no gain or loss [is] recognized if stock or securities in a corporation a party to a reorganization are, in pursuance to the plan of reorganization, exchanged solely for the stock or securities in such corporation or in another corporation a party to the reorganization." Also, under section (b) (4) no loss or gain is recognized when a corporation a party to a reorganization, exchanges property, in pursuance to the reorganization plan, solely for the stock or securities in another corporation a party to the reorganization. 

Under subsection (b) (6) of section 112 no gain or loss is recognized "upon the receipt by a corporation of property distributed in complete liquidation of another corporation."

"If an exchange would be within the provisions of Subsection (b) (4) of this section if it were not for the fact that the property received in exchange consists not only of stock or securities * but also of other property or money," then no gain will be recognized if the corporation distributes such property or money in pursuance of the reorganization plan. If the exchange is recognized as a gain to the corporation, the amount of the gain for taxation purposes shall not be "in excess of the sum of such money and a fair market value of such other property so received, which is not so distributed." "Reorganization" as used in this section means "(A) a statutory merger or consolidation, or (B) the acquisition by one corporation, in exchange solely for all or a part of its voting stock, of at least 80 per centum of the voting stock and at least 80 per centum of the total number of shares of all of the classes of stock of another corporation, or (C) the acquisition of one corporation, in exchange solely for all or a part of its voting stock, of substantially all the properties of another corporation, or (D) a transfer by a corporation of all or a part of its assets to another corporation if immediately after the transfer the transferor or its shareholders or both are in control of the corporation to which the assets are transferred, or (E) a recapitalization, or (F) a mere change in identity, form, or place of organization, however effected." The term "a party to the reorganization" as used in this section "includes a corporation resulting from a reorganization" as well as both corporations when a reorganization results from the "acquisition by one corporation of a stock or properties of another." 50
